course.title: Software Testing and Quality
course.description: How to decide what to test, write tests that can fail for the right reasons, and judge a suite and a release by evidence instead of habit.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read and write basic Python, as taught in the existing courses, and has built or maintained small programs.

paragraphs: A function that adds two 32-bit integers accepts 2^64 different pairs of arguments, and trying every pair at a billion tests a second would take centuries. Every test suite is therefore a sample of the inputs a program can receive, and a passing test reports only that the code gave the expected result for the input it was given. Software testing is the practice of choosing that sample, stating what each input should produce and judging what a green run does and does not show, and software quality is the wider question of whether a release deserves confidence.

Most of these judgements can be made with arithmetic and a careful look at a few lines of code. A rule that gives one rate to ages 18 to 65 can be tested with a handful of inputs, those just below, at and just above each edge, and they find mistakes that a hundred arbitrary ages would very probably miss. A suite that runs every line of a function may still check almost nothing, which shows up when small faults are planted in the code and the tests fail to notice them.

The same attention to evidence applies to the work around the tests. If each of fifty tests has a 1% chance of failing for no reason, about two runs in five will be red for no reason, and a team that has learnt to rerun until green no longer learns anything from a failure. Response times are better read as percentiles than as an average, because a few slow requests pull the average above most of the data, and the share of defects found before release compares what testing caught with what users met afterwards. Each of these numbers can mislead when it is read at face value, and knowing what it counts lets you say what a green run, a coverage figure or a response-time chart supports.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what a passing test does and does not show.
You'll be able to write a small deterministic unit test and run it.
You'll be able to choose inputs by partitions and boundaries.
You'll be able to compute coverage, mutation score, flake probability and defect detection percentage.
You'll be able to place tests at the right level and read percentiles and Little's law for performance.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Python for Data Analysis and How Computers Solve Problems: you should be able to read short Python functions, and a little SQL helps in one lesson.

modules.title: What testing can tell you
modules.description: What a test claims, how to write one, and how to choose inputs that matter.

modules.title: Techniques
modules.description: Measuring what tests exercise, isolating what they test, and finding what example-based tests miss.

modules.title: Strategy and non-functional quality
modules.description: Balancing test levels, testing data, speed and load, and measuring quality and process.

concepts.title: Test oracle
concepts.summary: The source of the expected result against which actual behaviour is compared.

concepts.title: Verification versus validation
concepts.summary: Verification asks whether we built it right against the specification; validation asks whether we built the right thing.

concepts.title: Limits of testing
concepts.summary: Testing can reveal defects but cannot prove their absence, because inputs are too many to try.

concepts.title: Arrange, act, assert
concepts.summary: Set up the inputs, call the unit, check one behaviour.

concepts.title: Deterministic test
concepts.summary: Given the same code it always gives the same result, independent of time, order or network.

concepts.title: Behaviour naming
concepts.summary: A test name states the situation and the expected result, so a failure explains itself.

concepts.title: Equivalence partitioning
concepts.summary: Group inputs that the program should treat the same and test one from each group.

concepts.title: Boundary value analysis
concepts.summary: Test at and next to the edges of each partition, where off-by-one errors live.

concepts.title: Decision table
concepts.summary: A grid of condition combinations and the expected action for each.

concepts.title: Line and branch coverage
concepts.summary: Line coverage counts statements run; branch coverage counts decision outcomes taken.

concepts.title: Mutation testing
concepts.summary: Small deliberate faults (mutants) are planted; tests that fail on them kill them.

concepts.title: Coverage as a target
concepts.summary: A number used as a target stops measuring quality, because tests can run code without checking anything.

concepts.title: Test double
concepts.summary: A stand-in for a real dependency; kinds include stub, fake, mock and spy.

concepts.title: Dependency injection
concepts.summary: The unit receives its dependencies as arguments, so a test can supply doubles.

concepts.title: Over-mocking
concepts.summary: Tests that restate the implementation break on refactoring and prove little.

concepts.title: Property
concepts.summary: A statement that holds for every valid input, such as reversing a list twice returns it.

concepts.title: Shrinking
concepts.summary: A generator reduces a failing input to a minimal one that still fails.

concepts.title: Exploratory testing
concepts.summary: Simultaneous learning, test design and execution guided by the tester's judgement.

concepts.title: Red, green, refactor
concepts.summary: Write a failing test, make it pass in the simplest way, then improve the design with tests green.

concepts.title: Refactoring
concepts.summary: Changing structure without changing behaviour, which tests must confirm.

concepts.title: Regression test
concepts.summary: A test written for a fixed bug so it cannot return.

concepts.title: Test levels
concepts.summary: Unit tests check one piece, integration tests check pieces together, end-to-end tests check a user journey.

concepts.title: Test pyramid
concepts.summary: Many fast low-level tests and few slow high-level ones keep feedback fast and failures local.

concepts.title: Flaky test
concepts.summary: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code.

concepts.title: Data quality check
concepts.summary: A query that asserts a rule about data, such as uniqueness, non-null or valid range.

concepts.title: Contract test
concepts.summary: A test that a provider and a consumer agree on the shape and meaning of messages.

concepts.title: Test data
concepts.summary: Small, deliberate, independent data created per test, never shared mutable data.

concepts.title: Percentile
concepts.summary: The p-th percentile is the value at or below which p per cent of observations fall; the mean can hide the slow tail.

concepts.title: Little's law
concepts.summary: Average concurrency L equals arrival rate lambda times average time in system W.

concepts.title: Non-functional tests
concepts.summary: Tests of performance, security, accessibility, reliability and usability, which have thresholds rather than exact answers.

concepts.title: Severity versus priority
concepts.summary: Severity is the impact of a defect; priority is the order in which it should be fixed.

concepts.title: Defect detection percentage
concepts.summary: Defects found before release as a share of all defects found before and after.

concepts.title: Shift left and right
concepts.summary: Test early (reviews, unit tests) and also observe production (monitoring, canaries), since neither alone finds everything.

lessons.title: What a test can and cannot show

reveal.text: The function returns True for 1900, because `1900 % 4` is 0, so the sixth test fails and five of six pass. The function was wrong all along, and the suite now reports it.

lead.text: Each row in the figure is one **test**: an input is given to the function, the result is noted, and the result is compared with the result that was expected. All five rows pass, and yet the function is wrong.

The second view shows why. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year *except* when it is a century, and a century counts only when it is also divisible by 400. The year 1900 is a century that 400 does not divide, so it was not a leap year, but `1900 % 4` is 0 and the function answers `True`. None of the five inputs was a century of that kind, so none of them could have noticed.

afterFigure.text: Five passes were therefore *true* reports, and each said exactly what it had checked: that the function behaves as expected at that one input. The mistake lies in reading five passes as a statement about all years. What a suite can honestly claim is limited by the inputs it chose.

lead.text: A test has three parts, and the figure labels them. The *input* is what the function is given, the *action* is the call to the function, and the *expected result* is what the function should return. The comparison between the actual result and the expected result is what produces a pass or a fail.

The expected result has to come from somewhere, and in the figure it comes from the calendar rule that centuries are leap years only when divisible by 400. That source is called the test's **oracle**. It might be a written rule, a table of known answers, a hand calculation, or another program that is trusted more than the one under test, such as Python's `calendar.isleap`. What matters is that the oracle is *independent* of the code being checked: if the expected value is copied from what the function currently returns, the test can never disagree with it.

afterFigure.text: Choosing the oracle is therefore the hard part of writing a test. Choosing an input is easy, but knowing what the correct output for that input is requires knowledge that the code does not have. When no oracle is available, as with a program that predicts weather, the tests have to be weaker.

reveal.text: A test is only as independent as its expected result. Here the expected result shares the code's factor, so the test passes whatever the specification says. Working the expected value out from the specification, 37.5, would have made it fail.

lead.text: An obvious reply to the leap-year fault is to test *every* year. But a function that takes two 32-bit integers, such as one that adds two numbers or compares two ids, accepts 2^32 values for each argument, and every value of the first can be paired with every value of the second. The number of pairs is 2^32 × 2^32, which is 2^64.
Each doubling of the width *squares* the count, and at a billion tests a second the pair of 32-bit integers takes several centuries.

afterFigure.text: Checking all inputs is called **exhaustive testing**, and for almost any real program it cannot be done. Edsger Dijkstra put the consequence in 1970, in his Notes on Structured Programming: testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence. A test suite is therefore a sample of the input space, and the useful question is how well the sample was chosen.

steps.headline: Work out how long exhaustive testing of two 32-bit integers takes at a billion tests a second.

workedSteps.text: Count the input pairs: each argument takes 2^32 values, and the pairs multiply.
Now divide the number of tests by 10^9.
A year of 365.25 days contains 365.25 × 24 × 3600 seconds.
Divide the seconds by the seconds in a year.

reveal.text: Sixteen million pairs is small enough for exhaustive testing, at about a sixtieth of a second at a billion tests a second. Whether exhaustive testing is feasible depends on the width of the inputs.

lead.text: Passing every test against a specification still leaves a second question open. A **specification** is a written statement of what a product should do, and checking the product against it is called **verification**: was it built right? The tests for `is_leap` verify the function against the calendar rule.

Suppose a tax form follows its specification to the letter, but the specification asks for gross income where people need the form to work out what they owe after allowances. Every check against the specification passes, and the form is still of no use. Checking that the product satisfies the need of those who will use it is called **validation**: was the right thing built?

afterFigure.text: A verification failure sends the team back to the code, whereas a validation failure sends it back to the specification and to the people the product is for. No amount of unit testing answers the second, because every unit test takes the specification as its oracle.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row: the user's need, the specification and the product. Verification is an arrow from the specification to the product. Validation is an arrow from the need to the product.
diagram.caption: Verification looks at the product against the specification. Validation looks at the product against the need. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The product matched the specification, so verification passes. Only watching real users, or asking them, would have shown that fractions were missing.

lead.text: If tests cannot prove correctness, it is fair to ask what they are for. Software Engineering at Google gives several answers. A suite gives *confidence* that the behaviours it describes still hold. It guards against **regression**, which is the return of behaviour that used to work after a change. It *documents* what the code is meant to do in a form that is checked every time it runs. And writing the test first makes the author see the awkwardness of an interface before many others depend on it.

Testing is also wider than running code. Reading a requirement and finding that two rules contradict each other is a test of the idea, done before a line is written, and the standard glossaries count reviews and other checks that never run the program as *static* testing.

reveal.text: A review is static testing: it finds the defect in a document without executing anything, which is usually the cheapest time to find one.

lessons.orientation: What a passing test establishes, where its expected result comes from, and why the number of inputs limits testing.
lessons.reviewLabel: What a test can and cannot show
lessons.nextAction: Write a small, readable, deterministic unit test for is_leap with arrange, act and assert.

blocks.text: A function named `is_leap` returns `True` when `year % 4 == 0`, and it is checked with five tests: 2024, 2020 and 2000 are expected to give `True`, and 2023 and 2021 are expected to give `False`. All five pass, and each pass reports something exact, that the function gave the expected answer for that one year. A run of five green results is easy to read as the much larger claim that the function is right for every year.
What that larger claim is worth depends on two things the word pass does not show, which inputs were tried and where the expected results came from.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a passing test does and does not show, name the oracle in a test, and tell verification from validation.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing what a suite can claim tells you how far to trust a green run.

recap.keyIdea: A passing test shows that one input gave the expected result, and a suite is a sample of inputs checked against an oracle, not a proof of correctness.

blocks.text: A test pairs an input with an expected result drawn from an independent **oracle**, and the 2^64 input pairs of even a two-argument function mean that a suite can only sample. Verification checks the product against its specification and validation checks it against the need, so a suite can pass both the five tests and the specification and still describe the wrong thing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson writes a first unit test for is_leap, names it by behaviour and makes it fail on purpose.

lessons.title: Writing a good unit test

lead.text: The test in the figure has three lines, and each does one job. The first, `year = 1900`, **arranges** the test by setting up what the code needs, here a single input. The second, `result = is_leap(year)`, **acts**: it calls the code under test, and only once. The third, `assert result is False`, **asserts**, which means that it states what must be true of the result. This division is called *arrange, act, assert*, and tests that follow it can be read in seconds because the reader always knows which line is which.

If the condition after `assert` is false, Python raises an **AssertionError**, which stops the test and is reported as a failure. The word *unit* in unit test refers to the size of the thing under test, a function or a small class, in contrast with a whole program.

afterFigure.text: Keep the act line to a single call. When a test calls the code twice and checks something at the end, a failure leaves you guessing which call caused it.

diagram.alt: A test function named test_century_not_divisible_by_400_is_not_leap with three lines in its body: year = 1900, result = is_leap(year) and assert result is False. In the second view the lines are labelled arrange, act and assert.

reveal.text: A false assert raises AssertionError, and the text after the comma travels inside it. The next screen shows how that text appears when nothing catches the exception.

lead.text: Run the check in the first view and nothing appears at all, which is how a passing `assert` behaves. In the second view the function returns `True` for 1900, so the condition is false and Python reports an **AssertionError**. The report ends with the message that was written after the comma in the `assert`, and the lines above it show the file and line number of the check that failed.

The message is worth writing because it is what you read first. A bare failure says that something was false, whereas a message such as “1900 is not a leap year” says what was expected, so that you can tell whether the code or the test is at fault.

afterFigure.text: Reading a failure means asking three things in order: which check failed, what was expected, and what was actually returned.

diagram.alt: A line of Python, assert is_leap(1900) is False with a message. When the function returns True the run stops with a traceback that ends in AssertionError and the message. When it returns False nothing is printed.
diagram.caption: What a failed assert looks like. Use the buttons to compare a passing and a failing run.

reveal.text: The two failing tests are the two centuries that 400 does not divide. Tests at 2000 and 2023 pass against the broken function, so they cannot tell it apart from the correct one.

lead.text: Under the name `test1` the report says that something failed and leaves you to open the file. Under `test_century_not_divisible_by_400_is_not_leap` it says that a century not divisible by 400 was expected not to be a leap year, which is the *situation* and the *expected result* together. A name that carries both is a **behaviour name**.

Behaviour names have a second use, which is that a list of them reads as a specification of the code. A reader who scans the names of the tests for an order form, such as `rejects_negative_quantity`, `accepts_zero_discount` and `totals_include_postage`, learns what the form does without reading any body.

afterFigure.text: Names also expose tests that try to do too much. If a name needs the word and, such as `accepts_valid_dates_and_rejects_empty`, the test is checking two behaviours and is better split in two.

cases.label: A vague name

cases.label: A behaviour name
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><defs><marker id="g6" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="36" text-anchor="middle">The line a failing run prints</text><rect class="f-error-soft s-error w2" x="24" y="60" width="592" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="320.0" y="93.0" text-anchor="middle">FAILED test_century_not_divisible_by_400_is_not_leap</text><text class="t" x="320" y="160" text-anchor="middle">The name already says the situation (a century not divisible by 400)</text><text class="t" x="320" y="190" text-anchor="middle">and the expected result (not a leap year).</text><text class="t-bold t-green" x="320" y="240" text-anchor="middle">You know where to look before opening the file.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The chosen name gives the situation and the expected result. Each of the others gives only one of them, or neither.
The exception ends the test at the second line. The third check never runs, so a test with many asserts reports only its first failure.

lead.text: Because a failed assert ends the test, a test with several asserts reports only the first problem and hides the rest. A test with a single behaviour has a single reason to fail, so a failure points to one cause.

A test that asserts the *behaviour*, such as the value returned for 1900, keeps passing when the code inside is rewritten, provided the answer stays the same. A test that reaches into the internals, checking which helper was called or what a private variable holds, fails when the code is tidied even though nothing visible has changed.

afterFigure.text: Failures of this second kind teach people to distrust the suite, because a red result no longer signals a defect.

lead.text: A passing test is only good evidence if the test would have failed on wrong code. Some tests cannot: an assert whose condition is always true, a test whose body never runs because of a typing slip in its name, or a comparison of a value with itself. All of them are green and all of them check nothing.

The remedy is to see the test fail on purpose. Write the test, run it against code that is deliberately wrong, such as the version that tests only `year % 4 == 0`, and watch it fail with the message you expect. This is called the **red step**, since test runners show a failure in red. Then run it against the correct code and watch it pass. A test that has been seen to go red for the right reason has shown that it can tell good code from bad.

afterFigure.text: The check takes under a minute and is most worth doing for a test that was written *after* the code, when the code already passes and nothing has ever made the test fail.

diagram.alt: A test box and a code box with an arrow between them. With the code as written the result is green and the test passes. With the code broken on purpose, by using year % 4 == 0 alone, the result is red and the test fails.

steps.headline: Add a test for 2100 and show that it can fail.

workedSteps.text: Write the test with a behaviour name, one input and one assert.
workedSteps.math: def test_2100_is_not_leap(): assert is_leap(2100) is False

workedSteps.text: Run it against the deliberately broken function `year % 4 == 0`. The function returns `True` for 2100, so the assert fails.
Replace the body with the corrected rule, `year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)`, and run the test again.
workedSteps.math: 2100 % 100 != 0 is False and 2100 % 400 == 0 is False, so the result is False

workedSteps.text: The result is False, which equals the expected value, so the test passes: red against the broken code, green against the correct code.

lead.text: A test is **deterministic** when, for the same code, it always gives the same result. The test in the figure reads the current year inside `age_in_years`, so it passes through 2026 and fails on 1 January 2027 although no line of code has changed. The same happens when a test uses random numbers without a fixed seed, depends on running after another test, or calls a network service that is sometimes slow.

The cure is to turn each hidden input into an *argument*, as the second view does: `age_in_years(born, today)` takes the date as a parameter, and the test supplies `date(2026, 6, 1)`. A random generator can be given a fixed seed so that it produces the same numbers every run.

afterFigure.text: Non-deterministic tests are damaging because the failures cannot be reproduced, and a failure that cannot be reproduced is soon ignored.

reveal.text: The test's expected value, 36, was right for 2026 only. Supplying the date as an argument would have kept the answer at 36 for the date given.

lessons.orientation: Write a test with arrange, act and assert, name it by behaviour and make it deterministic.
lessons.nextAction: Choose test inputs by equivalence partitions and boundaries instead of by guesswork.

blocks.text: The leap-year rule, once corrected, is `year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)`, and it should give `False` for 1900. Python's `assert` statement turns that expectation into something a program can check: if the condition after `assert` is true nothing happens, and if it is false the program stops with an `AssertionError`.

A test written with assert is an ordinary function, and nearly every good unit test has the same shape: it sets up an input, calls the code under test once, and states what must be true of the result, under a name that says which situation it covers.

diagram.alt: A test function named test_century_not_divisible_by_400_is_not_leap with three lines in its body: year = 1900, result = is_leap(year) and assert result is False. In the second view the lines are labelled arrange, act and assert.
diagram.caption: A unit test in three lines. Use the buttons to label the three parts.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a small unit test with assert, name it by behaviour, run it and read the failure, and remove hidden inputs such as the clock.
intro.whyItMatters: A readable test that is seen to fail first is far more useful than one that merely passes.

recap.keyIdea: A good unit test arranges its input, acts once, asserts one behaviour under a name that states it, and has been seen to fail, with no hidden dependence on time or order.

blocks.text: You wrote tests with assert, read an AssertionError from the bottom up, and saw that a failed assert ends the test, so one behaviour per test keeps every failure visible. A test is trustworthy once it has been seen to go red for the right reason and cannot be changed by the date or by the order in which tests run.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks which inputs to give such tests, so that a handful of them can stand for the thousands that cannot be run.

lessons.title: Choosing inputs: partitions and boundaries

reveal.text: None fail, which is why testing at ages like these gives false comfort. The next screen starts from this observation.

lead.text: A group of inputs that the specification says should behave alike is called an **equivalence class**. If the program really does treat the members alike, one test in the class tells you about all of them, since a second member would take the same path through the code.

Choosing a single representative from each class is called **equivalence partitioning**. It replaces the question “which ages should I try?”, which has a hundred answers, with “what are the classes?”, which has three. The figure's second view marks one age in each class, 10, 40 and 80, and those three tests do cover every kind of behaviour the rule describes.

afterFigure.text: The word *represent* is carrying an assumption, which is that members of a class behave alike, and the assumption comes from the specification, not from the code. A mistake in the code can still make one member of a class behave differently, and the previous screen's mistaken comparison does exactly that to two values, 18 and 65.

reveal.text: The count of values in a class does not matter; what matters is the number of classes. The values at the edges of classes are looked at next.

lead.text: The figure's second view shows the mistake from the first screen. Replacing `>=` with `>` moves the start of the standard rate from 18 to 19, so exactly one value, 18, is handled wrongly. Tests in the middle of a class cannot see this, because the correct and mistaken code agree on 10, 40 and 80. A value exactly at an edge is called a **boundary value**, and it is here that a mistake in a comparison changes the result.

**Boundary value analysis** tests the values at and next to each edge. For ages 18 to 65 inclusive, the edges are 18 and 65, and the *two-value* method takes the edge and the value just outside it: 17 and 18 at one end, 65 and 66 at the other, which gives four tests. The *three-value* method adds the value just inside each edge, 19 and 64.

afterFigure.text: Glenford Myers popularised both techniques in The Art of Software Testing in 1979. Their appeal is the cost: four tests find every one-off error in the two comparisons, where a hundred random ages would very probably find none.

reveal.text: A boundary value is a value where the behaviour changes, such as 50 here. Tests in the middle of a class agree with the faulty code, and the test at the edge does not.

steps.headline: List the boundary tests for ages 18 to 65 inclusive, with the three-value method.

workedSteps.text: Find the edges of the valid class. The standard rate begins at 18 and ends at 65.
Take the value just outside each edge, which is where a wrong comparison puts a value on the wrong side.
Take the value just inside each edge for the three-value method.
Combine the edge values with their neighbours and count them, checking that no value appears twice.

lead.text: A rule says what to do with good input, and it usually says nothing about the rest, yet the rest arrives. For an age field, a negative number, text such as `"abc"` and an empty value are all inputs that the program must do *something* with, and each is a separate class because the program should respond to each differently, for instance with an error message.

The edges of the valid range are not the only boundaries either. Zero is a boundary because the sign of the number changes there. The largest number the field can hold is a boundary because arithmetic can overflow. Anywhere the behaviour changes is a place to test on both sides of the change.

afterFigure.text: So the test set for the age rule has valid classes with their boundary values and invalid classes with at least one value each.

diagram.alt: Boxes for the age classes. The first view shows three valid classes: under 18, 18 to 65 and over 65. The second adds three invalid classes: a negative number, text that is not a number, and empty input.
diagram.caption: Valid classes come from the rule; invalid classes come from asking what else could arrive. Use the buttons to add them.

reveal.text: A test set built from the valid classes and their boundaries can pass completely while the program crashes on an empty field, because empty input is a class of its own that none of those tests reaches. Each invalid class needs a test with its own expected result, such as an error message.

lead.text: Rules often combine several conditions, such as a loan that is approved only when the applicant is employed *and* has an income of at least 20,000. A **decision table** has one column for each combination of the conditions, with the action each combination should produce, and the figure shows one for two conditions.

The table makes the rule complete, since a missing column shows a combination that the specification forgot, and it makes the tests easy to choose, because each column is one test. It also shows the cost of combining conditions: each one doubles the number of columns, so three conditions give eight combinations.

diagram.alt: A decision table for a loan rule. With two conditions, employed and income of at least 20,000, there are four columns of yes and no. Approve needs both yes, refer when employed with low income, reject otherwise. With a third condition, no existing debt, there are eight columns.
diagram.caption: A decision table lists every combination of conditions. Use the buttons to add a third condition.

reveal.text: Each condition doubles the number of combinations, so five conditions give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 columns, and a table with ten has left twenty-two out. The count grows as a power of two, which is the same arithmetic as the input counts in the first lesson.
Counting edges first is the reliable way to count boundary tests: each edge gives two.

lessons.orientation: Divide inputs into classes, add boundary values, and tabulate combinations of conditions.
lessons.nextAction: Measure how much of the code a test set runs, and ask whether that number can be trusted.

blocks.text: A pricing rule gives the standard rate to ages 18 to 65 inclusive, and the age field will accept any whole number that someone types into it. A test can try only a handful of those numbers, so which ones are chosen matters more than how many, because a mistake in the code usually affects only some of the ages and a test finds it only by using one of them.

Ages that the rule treats alike can be tried together, and the values at which its treatment changes can be tried one by one, so a short list of inputs can cover the whole rule and you can say what that list leaves untested.

diagram.alt: A number line of ages from 0 to 100 divided into three classes: under 18, 18 to 65 which pay the standard rate, and over 65. A second view marks one test age in each class, 10, 40 and 80. A third view marks 17, 18, 65 and 66, which sit at the edges.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose test inputs by equivalence classes and boundary values, and list combinations of conditions in a decision table.
intro.whyItMatters: A short test set chosen by class and boundary finds more faults than a long random one.

recap.keyIdea: Test one value from each equivalence class and the values at and next to each boundary, and use a decision table where conditions combine.

blocks.text: Equivalence partitioning replaces many inputs with one representative per class, and boundary value analysis adds the values at the edges, where comparisons go wrong. Invalid input forms classes of its own, and a decision table lists the 2^n combinations that n conditions give.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how much of the code a test set runs, and why a high figure can still hide a poor suite.

lessons.title: Coverage and mutation testing

reveal.text: The line under `if a` is skipped, so five of six lines run. The next screen turns counts like this into measures.

lead.text: A tool that measures **coverage** watches the code while a suite runs and reports which parts ran. **Line coverage** is the share of lines that ran: for `f(True, False)` it is 5 of 6, or 83%, since the line `r += 2` never ran. **Branch coverage** counts something finer. Each `if` has two outcomes, true and false, so the two `if`s in `f` give four, and a branch is covered only when its outcome has actually been taken.

The call `f(True, True)` runs every line, so line coverage is 100%, but both `if`s were true and neither false outcome has been taken, which makes branch coverage 2 of 4, or 50%. Branch coverage is the stricter measure for this reason, since reaching every line does not mean that every decision was tested both ways.

diagram.alt: A function f of a and b with six lines: r = 0, if a, r += 1, if b, r += 2 and return r. Three views show which lines run and which of the four branch outcomes, a true, a false, b true and b false, are taken for different sets of calls.
diagram.caption: Which lines and which branch outcomes a set of calls reaches. Use the buttons to change the calls.

reveal.text: The two calls differ at `if a`, but `b` is true in both, so the false outcome of `if b` is still untaken.

lead.text: Imagine that the second branch of `f` has a fault and adds 3 where it should add 2. The figure's first view runs `f(True, True)` in a test that makes no assertion. Every line runs, the test passes, and a report would show 100% line coverage. The fault is not noticed, because nothing compared the returned value, 4, with the expected one, 3.

The second view adds a single assertion, and the same call now fails and reveals the fault. The coverage figure has not changed at all, which is the point: coverage measures the *execution* of code, and an assertion is what turns execution into a check. A suite can therefore reach complete coverage by calling every function and checking nothing.

diagram.alt: A function f with a bug in which the second branch adds 3 instead of 2. A test that calls f(True, True) with no assertion passes with 100 percent of lines run. The same call with assert f(True, True) == 3 fails because f returns 4.
diagram.caption: The same call, with and without an assertion. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Both suites ran every line, so both report 100%, and only the one that checked the value noticed the fault. Coverage describes execution, and whether results were checked is a separate matter, which the next screen turns to.

lead.text: To find out whether a suite would notice a fault, you can plant faults and see. A tool makes many copies of the code, each with one small change, such as replacing `r += 2` with `r += 3` or `if a` with `if not a`. Each changed copy is called a **mutant**. The suite is run against every mutant, and a mutant that makes some test fail is said to be **killed**, whereas a mutant that every test passes has **survived**.

The **mutation score** is the percentage of mutants killed. In the figure one test, `assert f(True, True) == 3`, kills six of the eight mutants. The two survivors replace a condition with `True`, which makes no difference when both conditions were true in the first place. A survivor is a specific gap: the second view adds a test of `f(False, False)`, which kills both, and the score reaches 100%.

afterFigure.text: Mutation testing is slower than coverage, because the suite runs once for each mutant, but it measures the thing that coverage leaves out. A survivor can also be an *equivalent* mutant, one whose behaviour is the same as the original's, so a score below 100% is not always a gap.

diagram.alt: A table of eight mutants of f, each with the change made, the result of f(True, True) and a verdict. With the one test, six are killed and two, the if a becomes if True and the if b becomes if True mutants, survive. Adding a test for f(False, False) kills all eight.
diagram.caption: Eight mutants run against the suite. Use the buttons to add a second test.

steps.headline: Score the suite that has the single test assert f(True, True) == 3.

workedSteps.text: Run the test on the original code. `f(True, True)` = 3, so the test passes, as it must for the comparison to mean anything.
Run it on each of the eight mutants and note which make it fail. Mutant 5, if a replaced by if True, returns 3 when a is already True, so the test cannot tell it apart.
Mutant 6 is the same kind of change to if b. Every other mutant gives a value other than 3.
Count the killed mutants and divide by the total, as a percentage.

lead.text: Suppose a team is told that every change must keep coverage above 90%. The quickest way to meet the target is to add tests that call functions and assert nothing, since coverage falls only when code goes unrun. The number goes up and the suite improves little. This effect of a measure losing its meaning once it becomes a target is known as **Goodhart's law**, after the economist Charles Goodhart.

Mutation score resists this better, because a test that checks nothing kills no mutants. The sensible use of both numbers is as *questions* asked of a suite: low coverage says that code is untested, and a survivor says what an assertion should have caught.

reveal.text: The one outcome left is reached only by the value 0, a boundary of the kind the previous lesson describes. Coverage and boundary analysis tend to point at the same gaps.

lessons.orientation: Count lines and branch outcomes covered, read a mutation score, and see why coverage can mislead.
lessons.nextAction: Isolate the code under test from slow or unpredictable dependencies with test doubles.

blocks.text: Consider a function `f(a, b)` that sets `r` to 0, adds 1 to `r` if `a` is true, adds 2 to `r` if `b` is true, and returns `r`. It has six lines and two decisions, and the single call `f(True, True)` runs all six lines but takes only two of the four decision outcomes, because both decisions come out true. A coverage tool therefore reports the same suite as 100% on lines and 50% on branches.
Both percentages describe what ran, and neither says whether anything was checked, since a test that calls f and asserts nothing earns exactly the same numbers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute line and branch coverage, read a mutation score, and say why 100% coverage does not mean a well-tested program.
intro.whyItMatters: These figures appear on dashboards and in review, and knowing what they omit stops them being misread.

recap.keyIdea: Coverage shows which code ran, and a mutation score shows how many planted faults the assertions caught, so only the second says anything about the checks.

blocks.text: Line coverage counts statements that ran, branch coverage counts decision outcomes that were taken, and both can reach 100% with no assertion at all. Mutation testing plants small faults and reports the share the tests kill, which exposes weak assertions, and any measure that is turned into a target is soon met without being improved.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the problem of code that calls the clock, a network or a database, and how a test replaces them.

lessons.title: Isolation and test doubles

reveal.text: The test fails in the afternoon although the code never changes. The next screen shows how to take the clock out of the function.

lead.text: A thing that a unit relies on but does not itself contain is called a **dependency**: the clock, a network service, a database, the file system and a random number generator are the usual ones. Each makes a test slower, less predictable or both.

The second view changes `greeting` so that it takes the time as an argument. Handing a unit its dependencies from outside, instead of letting it find them itself, is called **dependency injection**. It can be as plain as an extra parameter, as here, or a constructor argument for a class, and it needs no special library.

afterFigure.text: Injection applies to anything that is slow, random or outside the program's control.

reveal.text: Once a dependency is an argument, the test can give it a stand-in, which is what the next screen classifies.

lead.text: Whatever the test passes in place of the real dependency is called a **test double**, by analogy with a stunt double in a film. Doubles differ in how much they do. A **stub** returns canned answers, so the test decides what the dependency says. A **fake** is a simple but working version of the dependency, such as a dictionary that stores users in memory. A **mock** checks the calls it receives and fails the test if they were not the expected ones. A **spy** records its calls and lets the test inspect them afterwards.

The kinds are easily confused, because tools often call everything a mock. The distinction worth keeping is what the double *does*. A stub or a fake supplies answers and a test then checks the *result* of the unit. A mock or a spy supplies a record of *interactions*, and a test checks that the right calls were made.

afterFigure.text: Use the real dependency if it is fast and deterministic, then a fake, and keep stubs and interaction checks for the cases where nothing simpler will do.

diagram.alt: A unit under test connected to a test double. Four views name the double: a stub returns a canned answer, a fake is a simple working version, a mock checks the calls made to it, and a spy records the calls it receives.

reveal.text: The object only answers with a fixed number, so it is a stub. The test then checks the result of the unit and not the calls made to the object.

lead.text: A user repository normally reads and writes a database, which is slow to set up and shared between tests. A fake replaces it with a Python dictionary: `add(user)` stores the user under its id and `get(id)` reads it back, all in memory.

A fake is more work to write than a stub, since it has to behave like the real thing wherever the tests rely on it, and adding a user with an id that exists must replace it, as in a table keyed by id. The effort is repaid, because one fake serves every test of every unit that uses the repository, and each test builds a fresh one so that no test sees another's data.

afterFigure.text: Because a fake has real behaviour, tests written against it check the *outcome* of an operation, such as the user that can now be fetched.

diagram.alt: A signup function connected to a repository. With the real repository it also talks to a database server, which is slow and shared. With a fake repository that stores users in a Python dictionary, everything stays in memory and private to the test.

reveal.text: A fake has to copy the real store's rules, here that an id identifies a single row, for tests that use it to mean anything.

steps.headline: Test that signup sends one welcome message to each new user, using a spy in place of the mail server.

workedSteps.text: Arrange: create a spy mailer whose send method appends each message to a list called sent.
Act: call the unit with the spy passed in as the dependency. The third call repeats a name, and `signup` sends nothing for a name it has already seen.
workedSteps.math: signup('Ada', mailer); signup('Grace', mailer); signup('Ada', mailer)

workedSteps.text: Assert on what the spy recorded, which is the outcome that matters to the user: Ada was sent her message.
The length of the spy's list is the number of messages that `signup` really sent.

lead.text: It is tempting to double every collaborator and assert that each was called, since that seems to isolate the unit completely. A refactor renames an internal helper and the output stays the same. A test that checks the output stays green, but a test that asserts the helper was called fails, although nothing visible changed. This habit is called **over-mocking**, and it makes a suite that fails whenever the code is tidied.

A test of calls also proves little. It shows that the code does what the test says it does, and nothing about whether the result is right, since a unit that calls its helpers perfectly can still return the wrong answer. Checking the result, with a fake or a stub supplying the dependencies, keeps the test about behaviour and leaves the implementation free to change.

afterFigure.text: Interaction checks have their place when the call *is* the behaviour, as when a message must be sent to a customer exactly once. Elsewhere, prefer the cheapest double that lets you check the result.

reveal.text: The mock stands in for the very method under test, so the assertion checks the mock's own return value. A double belongs in place of a dependency and never in place of the code being tested.

lessons.orientation: Replace a slow or unpredictable dependency with a double and know which kind to use.
lessons.nextAction: Find inputs by properties and exploration instead of by single examples.

blocks.text: Take a function `greeting()` that reads the computer's clock and answers `'Good morning'` before 12:00. Whatever a test of it asserts, the result will depend on the time at which the test runs, because the clock is a value that the test cannot set, and the same is true of code that reads the network, a database or a random number generator. A test whose result changes while the code stays the same cannot tell you reliably whether anything is wrong.

The remedy is to let the test supply such a value itself, by passing it to the code as an argument. What is passed in can be anything from a fixed value to a small working replacement, and the choice among them decides how well the test survives later changes to the code.

diagram.alt: Two versions of a greeting function. In the first it reads the real clock inside itself and the result depends on when the test runs. In the second the time is passed in as an argument, and the test chooses 09:00.
diagram.caption: The same function with a hidden dependency and with an injected one. Use the buttons to compare.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to pass a dependency in as an argument, choose between a stub, a fake, a mock and a spy, and say why asserting internal calls makes tests brittle.
intro.whyItMatters: Tests that control their dependencies are fast, repeatable and still pass when the code is refactored.

recap.keyIdea: Pass dependencies in, replace them with the simplest double that lets you check the result, and avoid asserting how the code works inside.

blocks.text: Dependency injection hands a unit its clock, network or store as arguments, so a test can choose them. A stub supplies answers, a fake is a small working copy, a mock checks calls and a spy records them, and preferring results over calls keeps a suite from breaking whenever the code is refactored.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes beyond single examples, with properties that must hold for every input and generators that look for counter-examples.

lessons.title: Properties, fuzzing and exploratory testing

reveal.text: The faulty function loses two items, and the one example never noticed. The next screen asks what the test should have claimed instead.

lead.text: For a sort function there is a stronger kind of claim, which holds for *every* list. The output is ordered, so that each item is at most the next. It has the same length as the input, and the same items. Sorting the output again changes nothing. Each of these is a **property**, and none of them mentions a particular list, so each can be checked on any list at all.

In the second view the faulty sort is run on `[2, 1, 2]` and returns `[1, 2]`: the output is still ordered, and still unchanged by a second sort, but it has lost an item, so two of the four properties fail.

afterFigure.text: Writing a property takes more thought than writing an example, because you must say what is true of *all* the outputs, without computing a particular one. That also means a property does not need an oracle for each input, which lightens the problem described in the first lesson.

diagram.alt: Four properties of a sort function: the output is ordered, has the same length as the input, has the same items, and sorting twice equals sorting once. A second view shows a faulty sort that drops duplicates returning [1, 2] for [2, 1, 2], so the same-length and same-items properties fail.

reveal.text: A property that holds on one list is not shown to hold on all of them; the rest of the work is to try many lists, which a program can do.

lead.text: **Property-based testing** pairs a property with a **generator**, which produces many inputs of the right kind: lists of integers, say, of different lengths, with repeats and negatives and empty lists. The Hypothesis library for Python works this way. It runs the test on many generated inputs, and if the property is false for one, it reports that input as a counter-example.

A first failure is often cluttered. The generator may have found `[5, 2, 8, 2, 9]`, where only the repeated 2 matters. A property-based tool therefore performs **shrinking**: it removes items and simplifies values, runs the property again after each change, and keeps the change if the failure remains. The figure steps through this, and ends on `[0, 0]`, two equal items, from which nothing more can be removed. That is the minimal input the developer is shown.

afterFigure.text: The shrunk input is also an explanation: two equal values are enough, so the fault concerns duplicates.

reveal.text: The smallest failing list shows the least that triggers the fault, here a fourth item larger than the first three. A tool that shrinks failures would end on a list of that shape.

lead.text: It may seem that random inputs make a failure impossible to repeat. They do not, because the generator is driven by a *seed*, and a tool records the seed, or the failing input itself, so that the next run starts from the same place.

Properties do not replace example tests, for two reasons. Some code has no simple property, and an example such as a tax calculation for a given income is the clearest statement of what the code should do. And an example documents the behaviour for a reader, which a property does not. The two work together: examples pin down the cases that matter, and properties search for the ones nobody thought of.

afterFigure.text: Fuzzing is the same idea applied with less structure. A **fuzzer** feeds random or deliberately broken input to a program, often a parser, and watches for crashes and hangs. It needs no property beyond *must not fall over*, which suits code that reads data from outside.

diagram.alt: Two pipelines. In property-based testing a generator makes valid inputs, they go through the code under test and a property is checked on each output. In fuzzing a fuzzer makes random or mutated input for a parser and watches for crashes, hangs or errors.
diagram.caption: Property-based testing and fuzzing differ in what they generate and what they check. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Write and check a property for a reverse function: reversing a list twice returns the original.

workedSteps.text: State the property without naming a list: for every list x, reversing x and then reversing the result gives x back.
Check it by hand on one list with a correct reverse. Python's slice `x[::-1]` reverses a list.
Now run it against a faulty reverse that drops the first item, `bad_reverse(x)` = `x[:0:-1]`. The first call turns `[3, 1, 2]` into `[2, 1]`.
Apply it a second time and look at the length of the result, which the property says should be 3.

lead.text: **Exploratory testing** is testing in which learning, test design and execution happen together: the tester uses what the program has just shown to decide what to try next. A session has a **charter**, a short statement of what to explore and why, such as exploring checkout with expired cards to find how errors are reported, and a **time box**, often an hour or so.

The figure sets this beside a scripted test, which fixes its steps and its expected result in advance. A script can be repeated exactly by anyone, which makes it good for regression, whereas a session finds problems that nobody thought to script.

diagram.alt: Two sheets. A scripted test case lists fixed steps, an expected result, an actual result and a verdict. An exploratory session sheet has a charter, a time box, notes and findings.
diagram.caption: A script is fixed in advance and an exploratory session is steered by a charter. Use the buttons to compare.

A generator that produces strings with all kinds of characters would reach this input quickly, whereas an example written by hand probably avoids it.

lessons.orientation: State properties that must hold for all inputs and see how generation and exploration find what examples miss.
lessons.nextAction: Write a failing test first, make it pass, and tidy the code with the tests as a safety net.

blocks.text: A test of a sort function usually names one list and its sorted result, as in `my_sort([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3]`, and that tells you what the function does for that list and for no other. Some statements, however, hold for every list there is, such as that the output has as many items as the input, and that sorting the output a second time changes nothing. A statement of that kind, which names no particular list, is called a **property**, and it can be checked on any list at all.

Because a property names no list, a program can check it on many lists that it generates itself, far more than anyone would write out by hand, and when a check fails it can shrink the failing list to the smallest one that still fails. Generated inputs cannot judge whether a screen is confusing or a message misleading, which a person exploring the program can.

diagram.alt: Four properties of a sort function: the output is ordered, has the same length as the input, has the same items, and sorting twice equals sorting once. A second view shows a faulty sort that drops duplicates returning [1, 2] for [2, 1, 2], so the same-length and same-items properties fail.
diagram.caption: Four properties that hold for every list, and what happens when a faulty sort is checked against them. Use the buttons to switch.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to state properties for a function, explain how generators and shrinking use them, and say what exploratory testing adds.
intro.whyItMatters: Examples check the cases you thought of, and properties and exploration look for the others.

recap.keyIdea: A property holds for every valid input, so generated inputs can test it widely, and exploration finds what neither examples nor properties were written to find.

blocks.text: A property is a claim about all inputs, which a generator checks on many and a shrinker reduces to a minimal failure, with a seed so the run can be replayed. Fuzzing applies the same idea to parsers with fewer assumptions, and exploratory testing, steered by a charter, adds human judgement.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson writes the test before the code, in a loop of red, green and refactor.

lessons.title: Test-driven development and refactoring

reveal.text: The pass shows only that `fizz(3)` gives `'Fizz'`. The test has never been seen to fail, so it may be one that cannot, which is why test-driven development has each test fail before the code that satisfies it exists.

lead.text: In **test-driven development**, usually shortened to TDD, the test comes before the code that it tests. The loop has three stages. In the *red* stage you write one small test for behaviour the code does not yet have, run it, and watch it fail. In the *green* stage you write the simplest code that makes it pass. In the *refactor* stage you improve the structure of the code while all the tests stay green.

The word *one* matters. TDD is sometimes taken to mean writing all the tests first, but the unit of the loop is a single test and a few lines of code, perhaps a minute or two of work. Kent Beck described it in Test-Driven Development: By Example in 2002, drawing on practices from Extreme Programming.

afterFigure.text: The simplest code in the green stage can be startlingly simple, a function that returns a constant, because the test only asks for one case. The next test is what forces the code to become general.

diagram.alt: A loop of three stages. Red: write a failing test. Green: make it pass in the simplest way. Refactor: improve the design with the tests green. The loop then returns to red with the next test.
diagram.caption: The three stages of test-driven development. Use the buttons to move round the loop.

reveal.text: The failing test is also a statement of the behaviour wanted, written before the code exists. The rule for multiples of 5 follows only once a test asks for it.

lead.text: The figure builds a function that returns the number as text, except that multiples of 3 give `'Fizz'`, multiples of 5 give `'Buzz'` and multiples of 15 give `'FizzBuzz'`. The first test asks for `fizzbuzz(3) == 'Fizz'` and fails because the function does not exist. The simplest code that passes it returns the constant `'Fizz'`. That cheats, but it is honest to the test, and it makes the next test necessary.

That next test, `fizzbuzz(1) == '1'`, fails because the constant returns `'Fizz'`, and passing it forces a condition on `n % 3`. A test for 5 adds the Buzz rule. A test for 15 is red in an interesting way: the function returns `'Fizz'` because 15 is divisible by 3, so the code needs a special case, placed *first*.

afterFigure.text: The order of the tests is a design decision. Choosing the next test is choosing the smallest behaviour that the code cannot yet show.

diagram.alt: Four cycles of building a function fizzbuzz. Each cycle adds one test that fails, then the smallest change to the code that makes it pass. The code grows from returning Fizz, to a test for multiples of three, then of five, then of fifteen.
diagram.caption: Four cycles, each with a failing test and the smallest code that passes. Use the buttons to move through them.

cases.label: Cycle 1

reveal.text: The test for 30 fails because the rule for multiples of 3 matches first. A failing test like this is the red step of the next cycle.

lead.text: After the fourth cycle the function works but has a special case that repeats the other two rules. The figure shows a restructuring: build the result from the Fizz piece and the Buzz piece, and fall back to the number when both are empty. For 15 the two pieces join to `'FizzBuzz'`, so the special case is no longer needed. This kind of change is called **refactoring**: altering the structure of code without altering its behaviour.

If a refactoring changes any result, it is not a refactoring but a change of behaviour, and it should be a separate step with its own test. The test suite is what makes the strictness practical: you make the change, run every test, and green means that every behaviour you wrote a test for is intact.

afterFigure.text: Refactoring belongs in the third stage, when everything is green, because a red test during a restructuring leaves you unsure whether the code or the tidy-up caused it.

diagram.alt: Two versions of fizzbuzz with the same behaviour. Before, a special case for 15 comes first. After, the Fizz and Buzz pieces are joined, so no special case for 15 is needed. In both the tests are green.
diagram.caption: The same behaviour with two structures. Use the buttons to compare them.

cases.label: Before
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><defs><marker id="t8" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="28" text-anchor="middle">Before: a special case for 15</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="50" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="72" text-anchor="start">if n % 15 == 0: return 'FizzBuzz'</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="88" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="110" text-anchor="start">if n % 3 == 0: return 'Fizz'</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="126" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="148" text-anchor="start">if n % 5 == 0: return 'Buzz'</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="164" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="186" text-anchor="start">return str(n)</text><rect class="f-green-soft s-green w3" x="120" y="230" width="400" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t-bold t-green" x="320.0" y="260.0" text-anchor="middle">tests: all green, before and after</text><text class="t t-muted" x="320" y="320" text-anchor="middle">The structure changed and the results did not.</text></svg>

cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><defs><marker id="t9" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="28" text-anchor="middle">After: pieces joined together</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="50" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="72" text-anchor="start">out = ''</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="88" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="110" text-anchor="start">if n % 3 == 0: out += 'Fizz'</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="126" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="148" text-anchor="start">if n % 5 == 0: out += 'Buzz'</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="50" y="164" width="540" height="32" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="62" y="186" text-anchor="start">return out or str(n)</text><rect class="f-green-soft s-green w3" x="120" y="230" width="400" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t-bold t-green" x="320.0" y="260.0" text-anchor="middle">tests: all green, before and after</text><text class="t t-muted" x="320" y="320" text-anchor="middle">The structure changed and the results did not.</text></svg>

reveal.text: A refactoring leaves every result as it was, so the tests that passed before still pass afterwards. Rounding, or a new rule for negative prices, changes results, and each of those needs a test of its own.

lead.text: A **regression** is a change that breaks behaviour that used to work, and a **regression test** is one that stops it from happening again. The cheapest way to write one is to apply the loop to the bug. Say a customer reports that a discount is applied twice: a price of 200 with 50 per cent off should total 100 but comes out lower. The first step is not to look for the fault but to write the test, `assert total(200, 50) == 100`, and watch it fail.

Then fix the code, and the same test turns green. Written this way the test has been seen to fail for exactly the reason in the report, so it is known to detect the bug, and it stays in the suite as a permanent guard. A test written after the fix, which passes the first time it is run, has not shown that it could have caught the bug.

diagram.alt: A four-stage timeline of fixing a bug with a regression test. A bug is reported, a test that fails is written, the fix is applied and the test passes, and the test stays in the suite.
diagram.caption: The life of a regression test. Use the buttons to move along the timeline.

steps.headline: Fix the double discount with a regression test written first.

workedSteps.text: Write the test from the bug report, with the numbers the customer saw.
Run it against the current code, which applies the discount twice. The first discount gives 100 and the second is applied to that.
Work out what the current code returns, and confirm that it differs from 100, so the test is red for the reason reported.
Remove the second discount from the function, so that total returns after, and run the test again. It now returns 100 and passes.

reveal.text: A regression test that fails on the old code, for any numbers, is the evidence that it will catch the bug if it returns.

lessons.orientation: Follow red, green, refactor on a small function and write a regression test before a fix.
lessons.nextAction: Place tests at the unit, integration and end-to-end levels by cost and speed.

blocks.text: A test that says `fizzbuzz(3) == 'Fizz'`, written before any function called `fizzbuzz` exists, fails the first time it is run because there is nothing to call, and that failure is where **test-driven development** begins. Instead of writing the code and testing it afterwards, you write a test for behaviour the code does not yet have, watch it fail, and then write the least code that makes it pass.
Working in this order means that the code grows only as far as a test asks, so code and tests arrive together and stay in step.

diagram.alt: A loop of three stages. Red: write a failing test. Green: make it pass in the simplest way. Refactor: improve the design with the tests green. The loop then returns to red with the next test.
diagram.caption: The three stages of test-driven development. Use the buttons to move round the loop.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow red, green, refactor on a small function and write a failing test before a bug fix.
intro.whyItMatters: A loop of small steps with a safety net lets you change code without fearing what it breaks.

recap.keyIdea: Write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor with the tests green, and begin every bug fix with a test that fails.

blocks.text: The loop of red, green and refactor builds a function one tested behaviour at a time, and the tests are what make refactoring safe. A regression test written from a bug report fails before the fix and passes after it, which keeps the bug from coming back.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson places tests at the unit, integration and end-to-end levels and asks what each costs.

lessons.title: Test levels and the pyramid

reveal.text: Fifty tests take two hundred times as long as a thousand. The next screens say why the levels differ so much.

lead.text: A **unit test** exercises one piece alone, such as the order logic in the figure, with whatever it depends on replaced by a double. It is fast, which is why a suite can hold thousands, and a failure names the piece. An **integration test** exercises several pieces together, such as the order logic with a real database, to check that they agree about how they are connected. It costs more to set up and run, and a failure points at the connection.

An **end-to-end test** drives a whole user journey through the real system, from the interface to the data store. It is the most realistic, since it checks what a user would see, and it is also the slowest and the least specific: a failure says only that something along the journey broke.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row: UI, order logic and database. A unit test covers only the order logic. An integration test covers the order logic and the database. An end-to-end test covers all three.
diagram.caption: How much of the system each level exercises. Use the buttons to compare the levels.

A failure says only that something broke.</text></svg>

reveal.text: A test needs as much of the system as the risk lives in, and no more. Here that is the query and a real database, which is the integration level.

lead.text: Unit tests are cheap, so many can be written and run on every change. End-to-end tests are expensive, so each must justify itself. Drawn with width for number of tests, the result is a **test pyramid**, with unit tests as the base, integration tests above and a few end-to-end tests at the top. The picture was popularised by Mike Cohn.

Arithmetic shows why. A thousand unit tests at 5 ms take 5 seconds, a time nobody minds waiting for. Fifty end-to-end tests at 20 seconds take 1,000 seconds, about 16.7 minutes, and a suite that slow is run less often, so mistakes are found later. A team that tests mainly through the interface has a suite that is slow, whose failures are far from their cause, and which often fails for reasons unrelated to the code.

afterFigure.text: The shape is a guide and not a rule. What it says is to test each behaviour at the lowest level that can show it.

diagram.alt: A pyramid of three layers with unit tests as the wide base, integration tests in the middle and a few end-to-end tests at the top. The second view inverts it, with many end-to-end tests at the top and few unit tests at the base.
diagram.caption: The same three levels with the weight in different places. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The level follows from how much of the real system a test needs, and the cost follows the level. The next screens come back to how a suite is spread across the levels.

lead.text: A **flaky** test is one that passes on some runs and fails on others without any change to the code. Each flaky failure is rare, so it seems harmless, but the chances add up across a suite. If each of 50 independent tests has a 1% chance of a false failure, the chance that all 50 pass is 0.99 multiplied by itself 50 times, which is 0.605. The chance of at least one false failure is therefore 1 − 0.605 = 0.395, or about 39.5%. Two runs in five would be red for no reason.

The cost is more than the wasted time. When red results are often false, people learn to rerun and ignore them, and the red that signals a real defect goes unnoticed. A flaky test that passes tells you nothing, and one that fails tells you little.

afterFigure.text: Rerunning until green is therefore not a remedy. It removes the visible failure and keeps the cause, and the suite's information is lost.

steps.headline: Work out the chance that a run of 40 tests has at least one false failure, when each test has a 1% chance.

workedSteps.text: Each test passes with probability 0.99, since it fails falsely 1% of the time.
The tests are independent, so the chance that all 40 pass is the product of 40 factors of 0.99.
At least one failure is the opposite of every test passing, so its chance is 1 minus that product.
Subtract, and write the chance as a percentage to one decimal place.

reveal.text: A test that depends on what ran before it passes or fails by order, which is one cause of flakiness. Giving each test its own list removes the dependence.

lead.text: Most flaky tests depend on something that varies and that the test does not control. A fixed sleep, such as waiting two seconds for a page to load, fails on a slow day. Shared data lets one test change what another reads, and a test that passes only after another test has run depends on the order. The real clock and the network add variation of their own.

Each cause has a remedy that gives the control back to the test. Wait for a condition to hold, with a timeout, instead of for a fixed time. Have each test create its own data, and set up what it needs instead of relying on a predecessor. Inject a stand-in for the clock or the network. A test that cannot be fixed at once can be *quarantined*, which means taking it out of the blocking suite while keeping it visible, and repaired within a set time.

diagram.alt: Four common causes of flaky tests, which are fixed sleeps, shared data, test order and the real clock or network, and a second view with a remedy for each.
diagram.caption: Where flakiness comes from and how to remove it. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The test depends on timing that it does not control. Waiting for the condition itself removes the dependence, where a longer sleep only moves the failure.
Moving a check down the pyramid saves its time and shortens the path from a failure to its cause.

lessons.orientation: Place tests at unit, integration and end-to-end levels by cost and speed, and compute the effect of flakiness.
lessons.nextAction: Test a query and a data set with checks, and use contract tests at service boundaries.

blocks.text: A test that calls one function, with its dependencies replaced by doubles, can finish in about 5 milliseconds, whereas a test that drives a whole user journey through the real system, from the interface to the data store, can take 20 seconds. The slow test also has far more that can go wrong for reasons unconnected with the code, since a slow page or a network fault can fail it, and when it fails it says only that something along the journey broke.

Where a test sits therefore decides how often it can be run, how quickly it reports and how exactly it locates a fault, and the chance of a false failure, small for any one test, grows across a suite in a way that a single test's rate hides. Knowing these costs lets you place each test at the lowest level that can show the behaviour, and work out how much run time and how many false failures a given mix of tests will bring.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place tests at the right level by cost and speed, and compute how flakiness affects a run.
intro.whyItMatters: A suite that is fast and trustworthy is run constantly, and one that is slow or flaky stops being used.

recap.keyIdea: Test each behaviour at the lowest level that can show it, keep the slow levels few, and treat flakiness as damage to the suite's information.

blocks.text: Unit tests are fast and specific, integration tests check connections and end-to-end tests check a whole journey slowly, so a healthy suite is a pyramid. Flakiness compounds across a suite, giving a false failure in about two runs in five at 1% for each of 50 tests, so a flaky test must be fixed and not rerun.

lessons.title: Testing data, queries and APIs

reveal.text: The count of surplus rows is the number of rows minus the number of distinct emails. That is simple for five rows, and the next screen shows how a query finds duplicates in a table with a million rows.

lead.text: A table can be wrong in ways that no program is at fault for, such as two customers with the same email, a missing value, or an amount outside its range. A **data quality check** is a query written to find such rows. The convention is that it returns the *violations*, so that an empty result passes and any row returned is a fault to inspect.

Other common rules are written the same way: a not-null check returns rows where a column `IS NULL`, a range check returns rows with an amount below zero, and a reference check returns orders whose customer id has no matching customer.

afterFigure.text: A shorter form counts the surplus rows, `COUNT(*)` − `COUNT(DISTINCT email)`, which is zero when every email is unique. For the four rows above it is 4 − 3 = 1.

diagram.alt: A customers table with four rows and the emails a@x, b@x, a@x and c@x. In a second view a check query groups by email and keeps groups larger than one, and returns a single row, a@x with count 2, which marks the violation.

reveal.text: A check query returns the offending rows, so an empty result means the rule holds. Here it returns `p@x`, which appears three times.

lead.text: A service's API is the set of requests that other programs may send, and testing it directly is quicker and more precise than testing it through a user interface that also uses it. For each request an **API test** asserts several things. The *status code* says whether the call succeeded, for instance 200 for a found order and 404 for one that does not exist. The *shape* of the body says which fields are present and of what type. The *error cases* check that a bad request gets a clear error and changes nothing.

A fourth check concerns repetition. A request is **idempotent** when sending it several times leaves the system in the same state as sending it once. Setting an order's status to paid with `PUT` is idempotent, and creating an order with `POST` is not, because each success adds another. Clients retry when a reply is lost, so a test that sends the request twice and compares the state is one of the more valuable tests an API can have.

afterFigure.text: A user-interface test that passes does not show that the API is right, since the interface may be hiding the error.

diagram.alt: Three API exchanges and what a test asserts for each. A successful GET returns 200 with a body that has an id and a total. A GET for a missing order returns 404 with an error message. Repeating the same PUT leaves the order in the same state as sending it once.
