reveal.text: The retries are harmless only for requests that are idempotent, and POST is not one unless it carries an idempotency key.

lead.text: Services built by different teams depend on each other's messages. The consumer reads a field called total, and the provider decides to rename it to amount. Each team's own tests still pass, because the consumer's tests use a stand-in for the provider and the provider's tests know nothing of the consumer. The break appears only when the two are connected in production.

A **contract test** closes the gap. The consumer states what it relies on, the field `total` as a number, and that statement is the contract. The provider runs the contract against its real responses in its own build. In the figure's second view the provider renames the field, the contract test fails at once, and it fails in the build of the team that made the change, before release. Contracts written by the consumers are called *consumer-driven*, and they let each side change freely as long as the contract holds.

diagram.alt: A consumer, a contract and a provider. The contract says the response has a numeric field called total. In the first view the provider returns total and the contract test passes. In the second the provider renames the field to amount, and the contract test fails in the provider's build.
diagram.caption: A contract between a consumer and a provider. Use the buttons to rename the field.

reveal.text: Each team's own tests pass, because the consumer's stand-in still returns `status`. Only the contract checks the real responses, in the build of the team that made the change.

lead.text: A test needs data, and where it comes from affects whether the test can be trusted. A copy of production data seems realistic, but it may contain personal information that tests should not hold, and it hides the case under test among millions of rows. A shared database causes the problem in the figure: test B passes if test A ran before it and fails if not, so its result depends on the order.

The remedy is for each test to create exactly the rows it needs. A *builder* function makes this cheap: `customer(email='a@x')` returns a valid customer with sensible defaults for every field the test does not care about, so that the test names only the detail that matters. The data is small, the test says what it assumes, and the order of tests no longer matters.

steps.headline: Run the uniqueness check on five customers and read its result.

workedSteps.text: The data has five rows, a@x, b@x, a@x, c@x and b@x. Group them by email, which gives one group for each different address.
workedSteps.math: a@x: 2 rows;  b@x: 2 rows;  c@x: 1 row

workedSteps.text: Keep only the groups that have more than one row, which is the `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` part of the query.
The query returns one row for each group that was kept. Work out how many rows the check returns.
The check returned rows, so the data does not meet the rule. Fix the data or the code that wrote it, and run the check again until it returns nothing.

reveal.text: Repeated-request tests are a short way to find handlers that quietly assume each request arrives only once.

lessons.orientation: Test a data set with checks, an API with status, shape and repeated requests, and service boundaries with contracts.

blocks.text: A table can break a rule without any program being at fault, as when an order carries a customer id that no customer has. Every function that touched the table may be correct, yet the data is wrong, and no unit test of the code would show it. A query can show it, though, if it is written to return the rows that break the rule, because an empty result then means that the data passes and every row returned is a fault to inspect.

Between programs, the same idea applies to the messages they send. A request to a service has a status, a shape and a behaviour when it is repeated, all of which a test can assert, and an agreement between two services, such as the name of a field that one reads from the other, can be written down as a test that fails in the build of whichever side breaks it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a SQL check that finds rule violations, say what an API test asserts, and explain how a contract test catches a breaking change.
intro.whyItMatters: Data and interfaces break in ways that unit tests of code never see, and these tests find them cheaply.

recap.keyIdea: A check query returns the rows that break a rule, an API test asserts status, shape, errors and repeats, and a contract test catches a break between services before release.

blocks.text: Data quality checks return violations, so an empty result passes. API tests assert status, shape, errors and idempotence, and a contract test lets a provider find out in its own build that a change would break a consumer, provided every test builds the data it needs.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to how fast and how reliably the software runs, with percentiles, Little's law and load tests.

lessons.title: Performance and other non-functional tests

reveal.text: The mean rises by 200 ms, from 48.8 ms to 248.8 ms, although nineteen of the twenty requests did not change. The next screen looks at what describes the slow tail better.

lead.text: The mean of the twenty times is 48.8 ms, a number that no typical request resembles. Seventeen requests took 41 ms or less, and three took 58, 120 and 450 ms.

A **percentile** describes the tail directly. The *p*-th percentile is a value such that *p* per cent of the observations are at or below it. One simple definition, the **nearest rank** method, takes the rank ceil(*p*/100 × *n*) in the sorted list, where *n* is the number of values and ceil rounds up. For the twenty times the 50th percentile has rank 10, which is 19 ms, the 90th has rank 18, which is 58 ms, and the 95th has rank 19, which is 120 ms.

afterFigure.text: A statement such as *95 per cent of requests finish within 120 ms* tells a user what to expect and tells a team what to improve. Performance targets are therefore usually written as percentiles.

steps.headline: Find the 80th percentile of the twenty response times by nearest rank.

workedSteps.text: Sort the values in ascending order, as in the figure, and count them.
Work out the rank by multiplying the percentile as a fraction by n and rounding up.
Count along the sorted list to the 16th value. The 11th to the 15th are listed here, and the 16th follows them.
Read the value at that rank, in milliseconds.

lead.text: A different question is how many requests are being handled at the same moment, which decides how many threads, connections or machines are needed. **Little's law** answers it. If requests arrive at an average rate λ per second and each spends an average time W seconds in the system, then the average number in the system, written L, is L = λ × W. The figure's first view has 200 requests arriving each second and each taking 0.25 s, so 200 × 0.25 = 50 requests are in flight at any moment.

The law was proved by John Little in 1961, and it holds for any stable system whatever the pattern of arrivals, which is why it is so useful. The second view doubles the time to 0.5 s and the number in flight doubles to 100. This is the usual way for a slow dependency to exhaust a connection pool: nothing about the arrival rate changed, but each request now stays longer, and more of them are inside at once.

afterFigure.text: The law connects a test result to a capacity decision. A load test reports W at a given λ, and L is the number of slots the system must provide for that load.

diagram.alt: Little's law drawn as three boxes: arrivals of 200 per second, an average time in the system, and the number in flight. With 0.25 s in the system the number in flight is 50. With 0.5 s it is 100.
diagram.caption: Concurrency is the arrival rate times the average time in the system. Use the buttons to double the time.

lead.text: Performance tests apply demand to a running system and measure what happens, and they differ in how much demand and for how long. A **load test** applies the demand that is expected and checks the targets, such as a 95th-percentile time under 300 ms. A **stress test** goes beyond the expected demand, to find the **breaking point**, the load at which the system fails or its response time climbs steeply, and to see *how* it fails: whether it slows, refuses requests or crashes.

Two more kinds are common. A **soak test** holds a normal load for hours to find faults that grow slowly, such as a memory leak, and a **spike test** raises the load suddenly to see whether the system recovers.

afterFigure.text: All of these report in percentiles, not means, and they are best run against something like production, since a test machine with a different size gives different results.

diagram.alt: A curve of latency against load that stays low and then climbs steeply. A load test covers loads up to the expected demand. A stress test continues beyond it to the breaking point. A soak test holds the expected demand for many hours to look for slow decay.
diagram.caption: What load, stress and soak tests each ask of the same system. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: A target chosen in advance turns a number into a verdict. Here the 95th percentile is 340 ms against a limit of 300 ms, so the load test misses the target.

lead.text: Performance is one of several qualities beyond *what* the software does, together called **non-functional** and tested in their own way. A functional test has an exact expected result, whereas most of these are judged against a threshold or a checklist: the 95th percentile must be under 300 ms, the error rate must stay under a stated figure, the site must meet a chosen accessibility standard.

Security testing looks for ways that the software can be abused. Accessibility testing asks whether people who use screen readers, keyboards alone or magnification can use the product. Both are partly automated, and in both an automated tool detects only a part of the problems, so a clean report from a tool means that nothing it can detect was found, and manual testing by people covers the rest.

afterFigure.text: Because the pass condition is a threshold, the threshold has to be chosen before the test, from what users need. A threshold written after seeing the result is a description of the result.

diagram.alt: Four kinds of non-functional test with the question each asks and a typical pass rule. Performance asks whether it is fast enough, security whether it can be abused, accessibility whether everyone can use it, and reliability whether it keeps working.
diagram.caption: Four non-functional tests, with what each asks and how it is judged. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: Tools are good at catching what is mechanical, such as known weaknesses in a library, and weaker at judging how an application's own rules can be abused.
With ten values the rank for the 90th percentile is 9, so the single outlier at rank 10 is excluded, and it takes the 100th percentile to reach it.

blocks.text: Twenty requests to a service took between 12 ms and 450 ms, and a team that wants to say how fast the service is has to summarise them in a single figure. The mean is the obvious choice, but a few very slow requests pull it upwards, so that it describes neither a typical request nor the slowest ones, and a team that reports it would not see how long its slowest users had to wait.

Percentiles describe the slow tail directly, since each names a value that a stated share of the requests did not exceed, and a small piece of queueing arithmetic turns a response time into the number of requests in the system at once.

intro.whyItMatters: Performance claims are only useful when they are stated as percentiles at a stated load.

recap.keyIdea: Describe response times with percentiles, size capacity with Little's law, and judge non-functional qualities against thresholds chosen in advance.

blocks.text: The mean hides a slow tail that percentiles show, and nearest rank picks the value at rank ceil(p/100 × n). Little's law turns an arrival rate and a time into the requests in flight, and load, stress and soak tests ask different questions of the same system against a stated expected demand.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson turns to defects themselves: how to report one, how to count what testing found, and where tests sit in a delivery pipeline.

lessons.title: Defects, quality measures and testing in delivery

lead.text: A defect found by a tester is of no use until someone can fix it, and someone else must usually do it. The first view of the figure is a report that fails at this.

The second view reports the same fault so that it can be acted on. A short title says what failed and when, the *steps to reproduce* are numbered, the *expected* and *actual* results are separate, so the fault is a stated disagreement and not an opinion, and the environment and evidence are attached. Of these the steps matter most, since a fault that can be reproduced can be investigated, and one that cannot is usually closed.

afterFigure.text: A good report also stays on the fault. Guesses about the cause belong in a comment, because a wrong guess in the title sends the investigation the wrong way.

diagram.alt: Two bug reports. The weak one says it is broken and asks for a fix, with no steps, expected result, environment or evidence. The useful one lists a title, steps to reproduce, the expected and actual results, the environment and evidence.
diagram.caption: A weak and a useful report of the same fault. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The other additions can help, and the steps are what make the rest possible. Without them the developer cannot see the crash or tell whether a fix works.

lead.text: Two words are often used for the same thing, though they mean different things. **Severity** is the impact of a defect on users and on the product: how much harm it does. **Priority** is the order in which defects should be fixed, and it depends on impact together with other things, such as how many people see it, how visible it is, and what else is waiting.

The grid in the figure gives four examples. A crash in an admin report that is rarely opened is *high* in severity, since the program fails, and *low* in priority, because almost nobody meets it. A company name misspelt on the landing page does no harm to anyone's work, so its severity is *low*, but every visitor sees it and the fix takes a minute, so its priority is *high*. Payments failing for everyone is high on both.

afterFigure.text: Severity is usually set by the tester or reporter, who knows the impact, and priority by the person who owns the plan, who knows what else competes for time.

diagram.alt: A grid of severity against priority with four example defects. A crash in a rarely used admin report is high severity and low priority. Card payments failing for everyone is high on both. A misaligned icon is low on both. A misspelt company name on the landing page is low severity and high priority.

reveal.text: The lost order does more harm, so it is the more severe defect, but every visitor sees the date format, so it comes first in the queue. Severity and priority are separate judgements.
The share is a measure of how well testing did against what users eventually found, and the next screen gives it a name.

lead.text: The share in the figure is called the **defect detection percentage**, often abbreviated DDP: the defects found before release, divided by those found before and after release together. Team A found 45 before and 5 after, so its DDP is 45 ÷ 50 = 90%. Team B found 30 before and 20 after, which gives 30 ÷ 50 = 60%, and users met many more of its defects.

The figure comes with two cautions. The count after release grows for months, since users keep finding defects, so a DDP measured early is flattering and one measured later falls. And a count of defects found is not a measure of quality in itself: a team that finds many defects may have worse code or better testing, and the number cannot say which. The measure is a prompt for questions, such as *where do the late defects come from*, and the answers show where testing is thin.

afterFigure.text: The numbers can still be used to compare releases of the same product, for which the cautions mostly cancel out.

reveal.text: Team C's late defects are the ones to examine: each shows a kind of test that was missing.

lead.text: A delivery pipeline runs a change through stages, and the figure puts a kind of test at each. Moving checks to the start of this line is called **shifting left**, because a defect found while it is still a requirement or a line of code is cheaper to repair than one found after release.

Not every defect can be found before release, since real traffic has variety that no test set matches. **Shifting right** means observing the software in use. Monitoring shows errors and slow requests as they happen, and a **canary release** sends a new version to a small share of users first so that a problem affects few. The DORA research, a long-running study of how software teams deliver, uses a measure of this, the *change failure rate*, the share of deployments that need a fix or a rollback, which a team reads together with how quickly service is restored.

afterFigure.text: Neither end is enough alone. Testing early cannot predict production, and observing only after release lets the users find every fault.

diagram.alt: A delivery pipeline with four stages: commit with unit tests and review, merge with integration and contract tests, staging with end-to-end and performance tests, and production with monitoring and canary releases. One view highlights the early stages, called shifting left, and the other highlights production, called shifting right.

reveal.text: The practice needs monitoring to be useful, since the small group's experience is the evidence.

steps.headline: Rank four areas of a product by risk, to decide where to spend testing effort first.

workedSteps.text: Give each area a likelihood of failure and an impact of failure, each from 1 to 5. Payments score 2 and 5, login 3 and 4, search 4 and 2, and the colour theme 4 and 1.
Multiply likelihood by impact for each area to get a risk score.
Compare the four scores and order the areas from the highest score to the lowest.
The area at the top is tested first and in the most depth. Work out the highest score.

reveal.text: The measure applies the same division as the defect detection percentage, with the failed deployments as the part and all deployments as the whole.

lessons.nextAction: Use the whole course to decide what to test, at which level, and how far to trust the result.

blocks.text: A bug report that says only that checkout is broken gives the developer nothing to follow. It does not say what was done, what should have happened, what happened instead or which version of the software it happened in, so the developer's first reply will be a question, and the report can wait days for the answer.
A report that can be followed gets the defect fixed, and the defect then has to be ranked, because the harm it does and the order in which it is fixed are separate judgements.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a reproducible bug report, tell severity from priority, compute defect detection percentage, and place tests in a pipeline.
intro.whyItMatters: These practices decide whether what testing finds is acted on, and whether the figures are read fairly.

recap.keyIdea: A report with steps lets a fault be fixed, severity and priority are different judgements, and detection percentage and early and late testing show how well a team's testing is working.

blocks.text: Severity is the impact of a defect and priority the order of fixing, and a report that someone can reproduce gets fixed. Defect detection percentage compares defects found before release with all found, and testing is spread along the pipeline, early to find defects cheaply and after release by monitoring and canaries, with the most effort placed where failure costs most.

questions.prompt: The function `is_leap(year)` returns `year % 4 == 0`. Five tests of it pass: 2024, 2020 and 2000 are expected to give `True`, and 2023 and 2021 are expected to give `False`. A sixth test is added, expecting `is_leap(1900)` to be `False`. What does the suite report?
hints: Work out `1900 % 4` and decide what the function returns.
Compare that with the expected value, False.
A test passes only when its own actual result equals its own expected result.

acceptedIdeas: Five tests pass and the new one fails
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Five tests pass and the new one fails

questions.onCorrect: The sixth test fails because 1900 is divisible by 4 but is a century not divisible by 400; the five earlier tests never tried such a year.

misconceptions.feedback: `1900 % 4` is 0, so the function returns True for 1900 while the new test expects False, and the earlier passes say nothing about a year they did not try.
2000 is divisible by 400, so the function's answer of `True` is the expected one and that test still passes; only the 1900 test disagrees with the function.
Each test compares one input with its own expected result, so a new failing test does not change the outcome of the five that were already passing.

choices.label: Five tests pass and the new one fails
The first five tests fail as well, because the new test shows the function is wrong
Four tests pass and two fail, because 1900 and 2000 are both centuries
All six tests pass, because the first five already pass

questions.prompt:
The specification says a price includes 25% tax, and a developer writes this function and test.

`def total(price, qty): return price * qty * 1.2`
`def test_total(): assert total(10, 3) == 10 * 3 * 1.2`

Running `pytest` prints `1 passed`. What does that pass show?
hints: Where does the expected value in the test come from?
Work out what the specification's 25% would give for 10 × 3 and compare it with what the test expects.

acceptedIdeas: The test repeats the function's own factor, so it cannot check the 25% in the specification
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The test repeats the function's own factor, so it cannot check the 25% in the specification

questions.onCorrect: The expected value was written with the same factor as the code, so a mistake in the factor sits on both sides of the comparison. An oracle has to come from the specification or from a source the code does not share.

misconceptions.feedback: The code multiplies by 1.2, which is 20% tax. The specification would give 10 × 3 × 1.25, which is 37.5, and the test passes because it repeats the same factor.
Both sides run the same multiplication, so they come out identical. What weakens the test is where the expected value came from, and the comparison is fine.
Other inputs would not help while the expected value is built from the same factor. Every input would pass with 1.2 on both sides.

choices.label: The test repeats the function's own factor, so it cannot check the 25% in the specification
The function applies the 25% tax from the specification correctly, as the green pass shows
The test is unreliable, because `==` cannot compare results that are decimal numbers
The function is only correct for 10 and 3, because the test tries no other values

questions.prompt: Why does the working divide 2^64 by 10^9?
hints: Tests divided by tests per second leaves what unit?
Check the units: a number of tests over a rate gives a time.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing a count by a rate gives a time.

choices.label: Because the tests run in parallel, so the work is divided up.
Because 10^9 is the number of bits in each of the two integers.
Because 10^9 is tests per second, so the quotient is in seconds.
Because the answer has to come out as a power of two again.

acceptedIdeas: Because 10^9 is tests per second, so the quotient is in seconds.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because 10^9 is tests per second, so the quotient is in seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate already counts tests per second, and nothing in the working assumes that runs happen in parallel.
Each integer has 32 bits, and that is a separate figure from the rate of 10^9 tests a second.
The division produces a time in seconds, which has no reason to be a power of two.

questions.prompt: Checking all 2^64 pairs at a billion tests a second takes how many years? Use 365.25 days in a year and give the nearest whole number.
hints: First find the number of seconds: divide the number of tests by the rate.
Then divide the seconds by the seconds in a year, 365.25 × 24 × 3600.
About 31.6 million seconds make a year.
questions.onCorrect: At a billion tests a second the run would take about 585 years, which is why exhaustive testing is out of reach for even a two-argument function.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^64 ≈ 1.8447 × 10^19 tests at 10^9 a second is 1.8447 × 10^10 seconds. A year of 365.25 days has 31,557,600 seconds, and 1.8447 × 10^10 ÷ 31,557,600 ≈ 584.5, which rounds to 585.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of seconds, about 1.84 × 10^10. Divide by the seconds in a year.

questions.prompt: A function takes two 12-bit integers, and tests can be run at a billion a second. Can every pair of inputs be tested?
hints: How many values can one 12-bit integer take?
Multiply the counts for the two integers, then divide by the rate of a billion tests a second.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because there are about 17 million pairs, which take well under a second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because there are about 17 million pairs, which take well under a second

questions.onCorrect: There are 2^24, or 16,777,216, pairs, which take about 0.017 seconds at a billion tests a second, so for inputs this narrow exhaustive testing is feasible.

misconceptions.feedback: Exhaustive testing is out of reach for wide inputs, but whether it is feasible depends on how many values each argument takes, and 12 bits is narrow.

Every value of the first argument can be paired with every value of the second, so the counts multiply: 4,096 × 4,096 is about 16.8 million pairs, not 8,192, although that is still small enough to test.
Multiplying 2^12 by 2^12 adds the exponents, which gives 2^24, or 16,777,216 pairs, and not 2^144.

choices.label: No, because there are 2^144 pairs, which would take far longer than 585 years
Yes, because there are only 8,192 pairs
Yes, because there are about 17 million pairs, which take well under a second
No, because no function with two arguments can be tested exhaustively

questions.prompt: A calculator app matches every line of its specification, but the people who use it wanted to enter fractions, and the specification never mentioned them. Which check would have caught the problem?
hints: Does the product match the specification, or the need?
Which check compares the product with what users want?
questions.onCorrect: Validation compares the product with what users need; a product can pass verification and still fail it.

choices.label: Verification
Static analysis of the source
Validation
A unit test of each function

acceptedIdeas: Validation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validation

misconceptions.feedback: Verification would pass, because the product does match its specification. The specification itself is what is wrong.
Unit tests check the code against what the specification says, so they would pass too.
Static analysis examines the source for defects of form and does not compare the product with what users need.

questions.prompt: Before any code exists, a team reads the requirements for a booking system and finds two rules that contradict each other. What name is given to checking that finds defects without running a program?
hints: The word describes checks that do not execute the code.
It is the opposite of dynamic testing.
questions.onCorrect: Reviews are static testing: they find defects in documents and code without running them.

acceptedIdeas: static testing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Static testing, which includes reviews of documents and code.

misconceptions.feedback: Dynamic testing runs the program. Here nothing has been written yet.

questions.prompt: A function has 300 tests and every one passes. A teammate makes six statements about the function. Which does the green run support, and which does it leave open?
hints: Ask what a single pass reports, and then what it says about inputs nobody tried.
A pass compares one actual result with one expected result.

items.label: The function gave the expected result for each of the 300 inputs tried
items.explanation: Each pass reports exactly this and nothing wider.

items.label: The function raised no error on any of those 300 inputs
items.explanation: An error would have turned the test red, and none did.

items.label: The function is correct for every possible input
items.explanation: A pass covers the input it used, and 300 inputs are a small sample of all of them.

items.label: A year such as 1900, which no test tried, would also pass
items.explanation: Inputs that were not tried tell us nothing, and the first lesson's leap year fault hid in exactly such an input.

items.label: The expected results came from a source independent of the code
items.explanation: A pass does not say where the expected value came from. A value pasted from the function's own output passes as easily.

items.label: The function does what its users wanted
items.explanation: Passing tests check the code against what was written down, and only validation can show that it was the right thing to build.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The passes support that the function gave the expected result for the 300 inputs and raised no error on them. They leave open correctness for every input, years that were never tried, the independence of the expected results and what users wanted.

questions.onCorrect: A pass reports on the inputs tried and on nothing else. Correctness for every input, a sound oracle and the users' needs each need more than a green run.

questions.prompt: A team builds a form exactly as its specification describes, and every test against the specification passes, but the form asks for information that the people filling it in do not have. Which check failed?
hints: Which comparison involves the users' need?
The tests passed against the specification, so ask what the specification itself might have missed.
questions.onCorrect: A product that matches its specification can still fail validation when the specification asks for the wrong thing.

choices.label: The regression suite
Validation
The unit tests
Verification

acceptedIdeas: Validation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validation

misconceptions.feedback: Verification compared the form with its specification, and that comparison passed.
The unit tests used the specification as their oracle, so they passed with it.
A regression suite checks that earlier behaviour still holds, which is not in question here.

questions.prompt:
A developer cannot say what `slugify('Hello, World!')` should return. She runs the function, sees `'hello-world'` and pastes that into the test.

`assert slugify('Hello, World!') == 'hello-world'`

The test passes. What is this test good evidence of?
hints: Where did the expected value come from, and could it have been anything else?
A test with a value copied from the code compares the code with itself at a later time.

acceptedIdeas: Only that the function still returns what it returned when the test was written
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only that the function still returns what it returned when the test was written

questions.onCorrect: A test with a value copied from the code detects change and nothing more. The first output still needs to be checked against the specification or another independent source.

misconceptions.feedback: The expected value was copied from the function's own output, so the test would pass whatever the output was, even a wrong one.
No specification was consulted. The expected value came from the code, so the test says nothing about whether it meets a specification.
It can fail. If the function's output changes later, the test reports it, which makes it useful for catching change. It cannot show that the first output was right.

choices.label: That the function is correct for this input, because the test passes
That the function matches its specification for this input and for others like it
Only that the function still returns what it returned when the test was written
Nothing at all, because a test with a pasted value can never fail

questions.prompt:
`try:`
`assert 2 + 2 == 5, 'sum wrong'`
`except AssertionError as e:`
`print(e)`

What does this code print?
hints: The condition `2 + 2 == 5` is false, so the assert raises an exception.
The text after the comma becomes the message of the exception, and `print(e)` shows that message.

acceptedIdeas: `sum wrong`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `sum wrong`

questions.onCorrect: A false assert raises `AssertionError`, and the text after the comma is its message. `print(e)` shows that message, `sum wrong`.

misconceptions.feedback: `False` is the value of the condition `2 + 2 == 5`. The text after the comma is what travels inside the `AssertionError`, and `print(e)` shows it.
`AssertionError` is the kind of exception. Printing the exception object itself shows its message, which is the text after the comma.
The `except` block runs and calls `print(e)`, so the message is printed. Catching an exception does not silence it.

choices.label: `False`
`AssertionError`
`sum wrong`
Nothing, because the exception is caught

questions.prompt: These four tests are run against the broken function `is_leap(year)` = `year % 4 == 0`. They expect 1900 to give `False`, 2000 to give `True`, 2100 to give `False` and 2023 to give `False`. Which of them fail?
hints: Work out the function's result for each year, then compare it with the expected value.

acceptedIdeas: The tests of 1900 and 2100
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tests of 1900 and 2100

questions.onCorrect: Both failing years are centuries that 400 does not divide, which are the inputs that distinguish the correct rule from the broken one.

misconceptions.feedback: 2100 behaves like 1900: it is divisible by 4, so the function returns True, while the test expects False.
2000 is divisible by 400, so True is the expected answer there and that test passes with the broken function.
The function gives the expected answers for 2000 and 2023, so those two tests pass.

choices.label: The tests of 1900 and 2000, because both are centuries
Only the test of 1900
The tests of 2000 and 2023
The tests of 1900 and 2100

questions.prompt: A test checks that a checkout refuses a coupon code that has already been used. Which name best states what the test checks?
hints: Look for the name that says both the situation and what should happen.
A name such as `returns_false` could belong to a hundred different tests.

acceptedIdeas: `rejects_used_coupon`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `rejects_used_coupon`

questions.onCorrect: The name states the situation, a used coupon, and the expected result, that it is rejected, so a failure report explains itself.

choices.label: `used_coupon`
`returns_false_for_input`
`coupon_checks`
`rejects_used_coupon`

misconceptions.feedback: It gives the situation but not what should happen, so a failure report would not say what was expected.
It gives a result but not the situation, so the report would not say which input produced it.
It names the area under test and neither the situation nor the expected result.

questions.prompt: A test function contains three assert lines. The condition of the first is true, the condition of the second is false and the condition of the third would be true. What does running the test report?
hints: What happens to a function when an exception is raised and not caught?
A false assert raises an AssertionError at that line.

acceptedIdeas: One failure, for the second assert, and the third assert never runs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One failure, for the second assert, and the third assert never runs

questions.onCorrect: A failed assertion ends the test, so later asserts in the same test are never reached; one behaviour per test avoids hiding results this way.

misconceptions.feedback: A test function ends at its first exception, so it gives one result for the whole test and not one for each assert line.
The exception raised by a false assert ends the function at that line, so the third assert does not run and any fault behind it stays hidden.

choices.label: One failure, and the third assert runs afterwards, so a fault there would be reported too
One failure, for the second assert, and the third assert never runs
Two passes and one failure, with a result for each assert line

questions.prompt: Why run the new test against the broken function first?
hints: What would a test that always passes show you?
Ask what a red result on broken code tells you about the test itself.
questions.onCorrect: A test seen to fail for the right reason has shown it can detect that fault.

choices.label: To find out exactly which line of the broken function is at fault.
To see the test fail, which shows it can detect this fault.
To measure how much of the function the test covers.
To check that the corrected function passes afterwards.

acceptedIdeas: To see the test fail, which shows it can detect this fault.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To see the test fail, which shows it can detect this fault.

misconceptions.feedback: The test is run on code that is already known to be wrong, so it has nothing to say about where the fault lies.
Coverage plays no part in this step, and the working never measures how much code ran.
That happens in the next step, once the rule is corrected, and running against the broken function serves a different purpose.

questions.prompt:
A test passes through 2026 and fails on 1 January 2027, with no change to any code.

`def age_in_years(born): return date.today().year - born`
`def test_age(): assert age_in_years(1990) == 36`

Which change makes the test reliable?
hints: Which input of the function changes from one day to the next without anyone touching the test?
A test is reliable when everything its result depends on is fixed inside the test.

acceptedIdeas: Give the function a `today` parameter and pass a fixed date from the test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give the function a `today` parameter and pass a fixed date from the test

questions.onCorrect: With the date passed in, `age_in_years(1990, date(2026, 12, 31))` gives 36 on every run, and `age_in_years(1990, date(2027, 1, 1))` gives 37. The date belongs to the test, so the result no longer depends on when the suite runs.

misconceptions.feedback: That passes in 2027 and fails again in 2028. The test still reads today's date, which is the input that keeps changing.
That hides the dependence on the date and does not remove it. In any other month the test would fail.
A test that ignores its own failure can never fail, so it stops checking anything.

choices.label: Give the function a `today` parameter and pass a fixed date from the test
Change the expected value in the test to 37, the right answer from 2027 onwards
Run the test only in the month of January each year
Catch the `AssertionError` in the test and ignore it

questions.prompt:
`pytest` runs a test of the broken `is_leap` and prints this.

`>       assert is_leap(1900) is False`
`E       assert True is False`
`E        +  where True = is_leap(1900)`
`test_leap.py:5: AssertionError`

What does the line beginning `E        +  where` tell you?
hints: Read the `where` line as a short equation, with a value on the left and the call that produced it on the right.
The `>` line shows the assert that failed, and the `E` lines say what each side of it turned out to be.

acceptedIdeas: The call `is_leap(1900)` returned `True`, where the test expected `False`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The call `is_leap(1900)` returned `True`, where the test expected `False`

questions.onCorrect: The `E` lines give the actual value and the call that produced it, so you can compare it with the expected value on the `>` line before opening any code.

misconceptions.feedback: The `E` lines come from a failed assertion, and the report ends in `AssertionError`. The `True` is the value that `is_leap(1900)` returned.
`test_leap.py:5` is the line of the failing assert in the test file. The report says the fault shows up in what `is_leap` returned.
1900 is not a leap year, so `False` is the right expected value. The function disagrees with the test, and that disagreement is what the report shows.

choices.label: The test returned `True`, so it passed
The call `is_leap(1900)` returned `True`, where the test expected `False`
Line 5 of `leap.py` contains the fault
The test should expect `True` for 1900, because the function returns that value

questions.prompt:
A developer writes three tests in `test_coupon.py`, runs `pytest -q` and sees this.

`2 passed in 0.37s`

The third function is named `tset_rejects_expired_coupon`. What happened to it?
hints: Count the tests the report says ran and compare that with the functions in the file.
pytest decides which functions to run from their names.

acceptedIdeas: pytest never collected it, because its name does not start with `test`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pytest never collected it, because its name does not start with `test`

questions.onCorrect: pytest collects functions whose names start with `test`, so a slip such as `tset_` gives a function that is never called and never reported. A test that has been seen to fail would have exposed the slip.

misconceptions.feedback: The report says 2 passed, so two tests ran. A third passing test would have made the report say 3 passed.
A failing test is reported as failed, with its output. A function that pytest does not collect is left out without any message.
pytest runs every test it collects from the file. The third function was left out because of its name.

choices.label: It ran and passed, and pytest counts it together with another test
It ran and failed, and pytest left the failure out of its count of passed tests
pytest stops after the first two tests in a file
pytest never collected it, because its name does not start with `test`

questions.prompt: Century years go wrong in `is_leap`, and no test covers 2100 yet. In what order do you work to add a test that can fail and then fix the code?
hints: A test that has never failed has not shown that it can.
The fix comes after the red result and before the green one.

items: Write a test that expects `is_leap(2100)` to be `False`
Run the test against the broken function and read the failure
Run the test again and see it pass

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write the test for 2100 first, run it against the broken function to see it fail, correct the function, then run the test again to see it pass.

questions.onCorrect: Seeing the test fail on the broken code shows that it can detect this fault, and seeing it pass afterwards shows that the fix worked.

questions.prompt: A pricing function should charge the standard rate for ages 18 to 65 inclusive, but by mistake its code reads `age > 18 and age < 65`. It is tested at the ages 10, 40 and 80, each expecting the rate that the rule gives. What do the three tests show?
hints: Work out the rate the mistaken code gives for 10, for 40 and for 80.
Compare each with what the rule says.
Which ages does the mistake change?

acceptedIdeas: None of the tests fail, so the mistake goes unnoticed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None of the tests fail, so the mistake goes unnoticed

questions.onCorrect: The mistake moves the edges by one, and tests in the middle of a class cannot see it.

misconceptions.feedback: The mistake changes the result only for 18 and 65, the two edges of the standard class, so 10 and 80 still get the other rates, as the rule says.
Every age from 19 to 64 still gets the standard rate, so 40 behaves as the rule says; only 18 and 65 are affected.

choices.label: None of the tests fail, so the mistake goes unnoticed
The tests at 10 and 80 fail, because the mistake changes the rate at both ends
The test at 40 fails, because the mistaken code leaves out some of the middle ages

questions.prompt: A form field accepts whole numbers from 1 to 99 and rejects every other whole number. Which set of test values puts one value in every equivalence class with the fewest tests?
hints: Each class needs at least one test.
One value represents the whole class.
questions.onCorrect: One value stands for its whole class because the program is meant to treat all of them alike.

misconceptions.feedback: One test covers only the class of accepted numbers; numbers below 1 and numbers above 99 are classes of their own, and the program should treat each of them differently.
1, 50, 99 all lie in the class of accepted numbers, so they test that class three times and leave the classes below 1 and above 99 untested.

questions.prompt:
A shop gives free delivery on orders of 50 or more, and the code reads:

`def free_delivery(total): return total > 50`

One order total is added to the tests. Which total makes the test fail and shows the fault?

The two can only disagree where the comparison changes from false to true.
questions.onCorrect: At exactly 50 the rule gives free delivery and `total > 50` does not. Totals such as 49, 51 and 100 agree with the rule, so tests there pass.

misconceptions.feedback: 49 gets no free delivery under the rule and none from the code, so a test there passes.
51 gets free delivery under the rule and from the code, so a test there passes.

questions.prompt: Ages 18 to 65 inclusive pay the standard rate. The three-value method tests below, at and above each edge, without repeating a value. How many tests is that?

Check whether any value appears in both lists.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The two edges are far apart, so their neighbours do not overlap and the three-value method gives 3 + 3 = 6 values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Edge 18 gives 17, 18 and 19. Edge 65 gives 64, 65 and 66. The six values are distinct, so 6 tests.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the two-value method, which omits 19 and 64.
9 would treat the middle and extremes as extra; the three-value method uses only the values next to each edge.

questions.prompt: The standard rate applies to ages 18 to 65 inclusive. A test set covers every class of valid ages and the values at and next to both edges, and every test uses a whole number. Which fault could the test set still miss?
hints: Which kinds of input does the test set never use?
Check each fault in turn, and ask whether any test in the set would reach it.

acceptedIdeas: The program crashes when the age field is left empty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The program crashes when the age field is left empty

questions.onCorrect: Invalid input needs an expected result too, such as an error message, and it is often where the defects are.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 lies in the class of standard-rate ages, which the test set covers, so a wrong rate there would make a test fail.
65 is one of the edge values in the test set, so a comparison that mishandled it would make the test at 65 fail.
Ages over 65 form a valid class that the test set covers, so a wrong rate there would show in the results.

choices.label: The standard rate is wrong for the age 40
The rate for ages over 65 is wrong
The program crashes when the age field is left empty
The comparison at 65 treats the age 65 as outside the range

questions.prompt: A decision table has one column for each combination of the conditions in a rule. A loan rule has five yes/no conditions, and its table has ten columns. What does that show?
hints: Each condition doubles the number of combinations.
Multiply the number of values of each condition, then compare the result with the columns the table has.

acceptedIdeas: Twenty-two combinations of the conditions are missing from the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Twenty-two combinations of the conditions are missing from the table

questions.onCorrect: Five yes/no conditions give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 combinations, so a table with ten columns has left out 22 of them.

choices.label: The table is complete, because each of the five conditions adds two columns
The table is complete, because combinations that give the same action can share a column
Twenty-two combinations of the conditions are missing from the table

misconceptions.feedback: Each condition doubles the number of combinations. It does not add a fixed two columns.

Each column stands for one combination, and a column left out can hide a case that the specification forgot. The usual answer to a large table is to split the rule into smaller tables, not to leave columns out.

questions.prompt: A bulk discount applies to orders of 100 items or more. Which pair of order sizes are the two-value boundary tests for this rule?
hints: How many edges does the rule have?
Take the value just below the edge and the value at the edge.
questions.onCorrect: A one-sided rule has one edge, so the two-value method gives two tests, 99 and 100, where a range has two edges and gives four.

misconceptions.feedback: 100 is the edge, but 1 is far from it; the two-value method takes the value just below the edge, which is 99.
100 is the edge, but 101 lies inside the discounted class; the value that detects a mistake in the comparison is the one just outside it, 99.
50 and 150 are representatives of the two classes, as equivalence partitioning would choose them, and they sit far from the edge where a mistaken comparison would go undetected.

choices.label: 1 and 100

questions.prompt: A form takes an age. The standard rate applies to ages 18 to 65 inclusive, and the valid classes are under 18, 18 to 65 and over 65. Which kind of test input is each of these?
hints: Ask first whether the value is an age at all, then whether it sits next to an edge or inside a class.
A boundary value is just below, at or just above the place where the rule changes.

items.explanation: It is the value just below the edge at 18.
It is the value just above the edge at 65.
It sits well inside the 18 to 65 class, so it stands for the whole class.
It stands for the class of ages over 65.

items.explanation: Text is not a number, so it is an invalid class of its own.

items.label: An empty field
items.explanation: The rule never mentions it, and the program still has to respond.

`def shipping(w):`
`if w <= 0: raise ValueError`
`if w < 5: return 4`

Look for the values that sit exactly on an edge.

acceptedIdeas: Weights 5 and 20, expecting 4 and 9
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Weights 5 and 20, expecting 4 and 9

Weights 6 and 21, expecting 9 and 15
Weights 5 and 20, expecting 4 and 9
Weights 0 and 100, expecting an error and 15

questions.prompt:
The specification says an age is a whole number from 0 to 120, and anything else must give the message `Enter an age`.

`def parse_age(text): return int(text)`

Which input does this function handle wrongly without raising any error?
hints: Work out which of these inputs `int` accepts.

questions.prompt:

misconceptions.feedback: `Miss` is 0, so every line ran. The arrow names one jump between two lines, and only that jump was never taken.

Suite A fails and suite B still passes
Both suites still pass, because line coverage is still 100%

No test uses the value 18, where the two comparisons give different results

    `if x > 10: return 10`

Count the outcomes taken and divide by 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the second decision as if the call had reached it. The call returns at the first `if`, so `x > 10` is never evaluated.

The test cannot read the users back afterwards, because a dictionary has no queries
The fake overwrites silently, so a repeated id that fails in production passes

A string with no spaces or underscores, such as abc
A string whose only separators are single spaces, such as a b c
A string that already contains an underscore, such as a_b c

questions.prompt: Which of these is a property of a sort function, rather than a single example?
hints: A property is about every valid input.
Which option would still be true after you changed the list you sorted?
questions.onCorrect: A property states something about all inputs, so a generator can check it on as many as time allows.

choices.label: Sorting a list of 1,000 numbers always finishes in under a second

acceptedIdeas: Sorting any list twice gives the same result as sorting it once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sorting any list twice gives the same result as sorting it once

misconceptions.feedback: That is one example of an input and its output, and it says nothing about other lists.
That is also a single example, an empty list.

questions.prompt: A team writes six checks for `my_sort`. Which are examples, each about one input, and which are properties, each about every list?
hints: Ask whether the check names a particular list or says something about all lists.
A generator can run a property on many inputs, and an example runs on its one.

items.label: `my_sort([2, 1]) == [1, 2]`
items.explanation: It names one list and its sorted result.

items.label: `my_sort([]) == []`
items.explanation: It is about the empty list only.

items.label: `my_sort([5, 5, 1]) == [1, 5, 5]`
items.explanation: It checks one list with repeated items.

items.label: For every list `xs`, `my_sort(my_sort(xs)) == my_sort(xs)`
items.explanation: It claims that sorting twice changes nothing, for any list.

items.label: For every list `xs`, `len(my_sort(xs)) == len(xs)`
items.explanation: It claims that no item is lost, for any list.

items.label: For every list `xs`, each item of `my_sort(xs)` is at most the next one
items.explanation: It claims that the output is ordered, for any list.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The checks of `[2, 1]`, the empty list and `[5, 5, 1]` are examples, and sorting twice, keeping the length and ordering every output are properties.

questions.onCorrect: An example holds for the one list it names, and a property is a claim about every list, which a generator can check on many inputs and which shrinking can narrow to a small failure.

questions.prompt: `clamp(x, lo, hi)` limits `x` to the range from `lo` to `hi`, where `lo <= hi`. For example `clamp(9, 1, 5)` is 5 and `clamp(3, 1, 5)` is 3. Which statement is a property that holds for every valid input?
hints: A property must hold for every input the generator can make, and a single example is not enough to show it.
Try a value below the range, one inside it and one above it against each statement.

acceptedIdeas: The result is never below `lo` and never above `hi`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The result is never below `lo` and never above `hi`

questions.onCorrect: Whatever `x` is, the result lies between `lo` and `hi`. The other statements fail for some input: a value inside the range comes back unchanged, and a value above `hi` comes back smaller.

misconceptions.feedback: `clamp(9, 1, 5)` is 5, so the result differs from `x` whenever `x` lies outside the range.
`clamp(3, 1, 5)` is 3, so a value inside the range comes back unchanged and is neither limit.
`clamp(9, 1, 5)` is 5, which is smaller than 9. A value above `hi` comes back as `hi`.

choices.label: The result is always equal to `x`
The result is never below `lo` and never above `hi`
The result is always either `lo` or `hi`
The result is always at least as large as the value `x` itself

questions.prompt: A developer writes the function `fizz(n)` = `'Fizz' if n % 3 == 0 else str(n)`, and then writes the test `assert fizz(3) == 'Fizz'`. The test passes the first time it is run. What has that pass shown?
hints: How many inputs does the test use?
Has the test ever been seen to fail?

acceptedIdeas: Only that `fizz(3)` gives `'Fizz'`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only that `fizz(3)` gives `'Fizz'`

questions.onCorrect: A test that passes the first time it is run has not shown that it can detect a fault, and seeing it fail first is what the red step is for.

misconceptions.feedback: The test uses one input, 3, so it says nothing about the other values of n.
The test has never been seen to fail, so nothing yet shows that it could; a test that cannot fail also passes the first time it is run.

choices.label: Only that `fizz(3)` gives `'Fizz'`
That the test would fail if fizz were wrong
That fizz is correct for every value of n

questions.prompt: All the tests of `fizzbuzz` pass. A developer now wants `fizzbuzz(5)` to return `'Buzz'`. What should the developer do first?
hints: The loop is red, green, refactor.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write the test for `fizzbuzz(5)` and run it to see it fail

questions.onCorrect: The failing test comes first, and seeing it fail for the right reason shows that it can detect the missing behaviour.

choices.label: Add the rule for multiples of 5, then write a test for it
Write the tests for 5, 10 and 20 before running any of them
Refactor the function so that a rule for 5 fits in easily
Write the test for `fizzbuzz(5)` and run it to see it fail

misconceptions.feedback: The code comes after a test that asks for it. A test written after the code passes on its first run and has never been seen to fail.
The unit of the loop is a single test and a few lines of code, so tests are written and run one at a time.
Refactoring is the third stage, and it happens once a test has gone green.

questions.prompt:

`def fizzbuzz(n):`

10 is not a multiple of 3, so the code reaches the rule for 5 and returns `'Buzz'`, and that test passes.

questions.prompt: All the tests for `total(price, pct)` pass. A developer changes the function and runs the tests again. Which change counts as a refactoring?
hints: A refactoring changes the structure of the code and not its behaviour.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Moving the discount formula into a helper function called `discounted`

choices.label: Making `total` round its result to the nearest 10
Moving the discount formula into a helper function called `discounted`
Making `total` return 0 when `price` is negative
Deleting the test for a `pct` of 100 so that a simpler formula can pass

misconceptions.feedback: Rounding changes the result for most prices, which is a change of behaviour. It needs a test of its own.

questions.prompt: The buggy function is `def total(price, pct): after = price * (100 - pct) // 100; return after * (100 - pct) // 100`, which applies the discount twice. What does `total(200, 50)` return?

Apply the same discount to after.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The test asserting 100 fails with 50, which is the red step for this bug.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first discount gives 200 × 50 // 100 = 100, and the second gives 100 × 50 // 100 = 50. The expected value is 100.

misconceptions.feedback: 100 is the correct value, which a single discount gives. The buggy code applies the discount again to that value.
The discount is subtracted as a percentage, not as a number of pounds; apply it twice.

questions.prompt: A customer reports that `total(300, 20)` returns 192, where 240 is right, because the discount is applied twice. Which test is the best regression test for this bug?

acceptedIdeas: `assert total(300, 20) == 240`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `assert total(300, 20) == 240`

questions.onCorrect: On the buggy code the call returns 192, so the test fails, and it passes once the discount is applied a single time. Tests at 0% or at a price of 0 cannot tell the buggy code from the fixed one.

misconceptions.feedback: That expects the buggy result, so it passes now and fails once the bug is fixed.
A discount of 0 gives the same result however often it is applied, so this passes on the buggy code and cannot catch the bug.
Zero stays zero however often a discount is applied, so this also passes on the buggy code.

choices.label: `assert total(300, 20) == 240`
`assert total(300, 20) == 192`
`assert total(300, 0) == 300`
`assert total(0, 20) == 0`

questions.prompt: All tests of `fizzbuzz` pass, and a developer adds the rule that multiples of 5 give `'Buzz'`. In what order does a test-driven cycle go?
hints: The test comes before the code it asks for.

items: Write a test that expects `fizzbuzz(5)` to be `'Buzz'`
Run the suite and see the new test fail
Add the simplest code that makes the new test pass
Run the suite and see every test pass
Tidy the code while the tests stay green

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write the test for 5 first, run it to see it fail, add the simplest code that passes, run the suite to see everything green and only then tidy the code with the tests as a safety net.

questions.prompt: A bug is reported and fixed. What stops it returning?
hints: What can turn red when behaviour changes?

questions.prompt: In the first cycle the only test is `assert fizzbuzz(3) == 'Fizz'`, and the developer makes it pass with `def fizzbuzz(n): return 'Fizz'`. Which test should come next to push the function to do more?

misconceptions.feedback: The constant `'Fizz'` already passes this, so the test is green at once and asks for nothing new.
A repeat of the same test passes again and adds nothing.

questions.prompt: Suite A has 1,000 unit tests of 5 ms each. Suite B has only 50 end-to-end tests of 20 s each. How does the run time of suite B compare with that of suite A?

Suite B takes a few times as long as suite A

questions.prompt: A developer writes a new SQL query that joins `orders` and `customers`. The risk is that a column name in the query does not match the real schema. Which test level checks that risk most cheaply?

misconceptions.feedback: A stub returns whatever it was given, so a wrong column name never meets a real schema.

questions.prompt: Each of 40 independent tests has a 1% chance of failing falsely in a run. What is the chance that a run has at least one false failure, as a percentage to one decimal place?

Subtract that from 1.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A rate that looks negligible per test becomes a failure in one run out of three, because the chances compound across the suite.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 40 pass with probability 0.99^40 = 0.669, so at least one fails with probability 1 − 0.669 = 0.331, which is 33.1%.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1% forty times. The chances do not simply add, since two false failures in one run are counted once.
That is the chance that all 40 tests pass; the question asks for at least one failure.

`def test_add_two(): cart.append('ink'); cart.append('pad'); assert len(cart) == 2`

misconceptions.feedback: pytest ran both tests as written. The extra item is the pen from `test_add_one`, left behind in the shared list.
`append` always adds exactly one item. The 3 comes from the earlier test, and the two calls add only 2.

choices.label: The tests share `cart`, so the second starts with the pen the first added
pytest has a fault that makes the second test count its own items wrongly
`append` is unreliable when it is called twice in a row

misconceptions.feedback: A longer sleep only moves the point where a slow day fails again, and it makes every run slower.
A retry hides the flakiness and leaves the dependence on timing in place. A real failure then takes several runs to show.
That loses the check. The test is sound, and it only guesses how long the export takes.

Run the test again automatically whenever it fails, up to three times
Delete the test, since a flaky test is worse than none
Wait until `export_is_ready()` is true, polling up to a time limit

questions.prompt: A test fails in the build and passes when it is run again, with no change to the code. In what order do you work to find and remove the flakiness?

items: Save the output of a failing run

questions.prompt: A team's suite has 40 unit tests, 5 integration tests and 400 end-to-end tests, and a run takes two hours. Developers often skip it. Which change would help most?
hints: Which level do most of the tests sit at, and what does that level cost?

misconceptions.feedback: More of the slowest tests would make the run longer still, and more flaky failures would follow.
Running it less often lets defects stay in longer. The slowness comes from where the tests sit.

questions.prompt: A suite has 200 independent tests, and each has a 0.5% chance of failing falsely in a run, with no fault in the code. Which figure is closest to the chance that a run shows at least one red result?
hints: Find the chance that every test passes, and subtract it from 1.
One test passes with probability 0.995, and the tests are independent, so the 200 probabilities multiply.
questions.onCorrect: All 200 tests pass with probability 0.995^200, about 36.7%, so a run turns red for no real reason about 63.3% of the time. A suite's flakiness grows with its size even when no test got worse.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one test. A run has 200 such chances, and any of them can turn it red.
Each test passes with probability 0.995, and all 200 pass together with probability 0.995^200. A run is red whenever any test fails, which is 1 minus that figure.

questions.prompt: A table of customers has five rows with the emails p@x, q@x, p@x, p@x and r@x. Each email is meant to appear once. How many rows must be removed to meet that rule?

questions.onCorrect: The count of surplus rows is the number of rows minus the number of distinct emails, here 5 − 3 = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows with p@x, and one of them should stay.
That is the number of emails that repeat. The email p@x has more than one surplus row.

questions.prompt: A table `c(email)` holds `p@x`, `q@x`, `p@x`, `p@x` and `r@x`, and each email is meant to appear once. Which query returns the emails that break the rule?

questions.onCorrect: Grouping by email and keeping groups with more than one row returns `p@x`, the one email that repeats. An empty result would mean that the rule holds.

misconceptions.feedback: It returns all three emails, `p@x`, `q@x` and `r@x`, whether they repeat or not. A check query returns only the violations.
It lists every email, the repeated one first, so `q@x` and `r@x` come back as well. A check query has to return only the emails that break the rule.
It returns 5, the number of rows. It names no email, and a count alone never says which rows break a rule.

choices.label: `SELECT email FROM c GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`
`SELECT DISTINCT email FROM c`
`SELECT email FROM c GROUP BY email ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`
`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM c`

questions.prompt: A client sends `POST /orders`, the reply is lost, and the client's network library sends the same request again. The server handled both requests. How can the API avoid a duplicate order?

misconceptions.feedback: `POST` is not idempotent. Each delivery can create another order, so two requests give two orders.
Waiting does not change what the server does with the second request, and it still creates a second order.
That avoids a duplicate and leaves the user not knowing whether the order exists. A key makes a retry safe.

choices.label: The server treats `POST` as idempotent, so a repeated request is harmless
The client sends an idempotency key, and the server returns the first order again
The client waits ten seconds before it retries

questions.prompt: A provider changes its response so that the field `status` is left out whenever an order has been cancelled. A consumer reads `status` from every response. Which test would catch this in the provider's build, before release?
