answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A contract test of the response

questions.onCorrect: A contract test fails in the provider's build when a real response no longer matches what a consumer expects.

choices.label: A contract test of the response
A usability test with real users
A load test at peak demand
A unit test of the consumer with a stand-in provider

misconceptions.feedback: A usability test examines how people use the product, which is not where a missing field is found.
A load test measures behaviour under demand, and it does not compare the fields of a response.
The stand-in still returns `status`, so the consumer's tests keep passing whatever the real provider does.

questions.prompt: Run the check on the five rows a@x, b@x, a@x, c@x and b@x. `SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;` How many rows does it return?
hints: Which groups have more than one row?
Count those groups, not the rows inside them.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The query returns one row per duplicated email, not one row per surplus customer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The groups a@x and b@x each have more than one row, so the check returns 2 rows.

misconceptions.feedback: The groups a@x and b@x hold four customers between them, but the query returns one row for each group.
A result of zero would mean the rule holds, and both a@x and b@x appear twice.

questions.prompt: The handler for `PUT /users/7` adds a row to a `history` table every time it runs, and the specification says that repeating the request must leave the same state. Which API test finds the fault?
hints: The specification is about repeating a request, so the test has to repeat one.
Compare the state after one delivery with the state after two.

acceptedIdeas: Send the same `PUT` twice and assert that the state equals the state after one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Send the same `PUT` twice and assert that the state equals the state after one

questions.onCorrect: Repeating the same request and comparing the state is the direct test of the rule, and it fails here because the second delivery adds a second `history` row.

misconceptions.feedback: A single request returns 200 whatever the handler does with repeats.
Different bodies change the state in either case. The fault shows only when the same request is repeated.
That checks one delivery. The extra row appears only on the second.

choices.label: Send one `PUT` and assert that the status is 200
Send two different `PUT` bodies and assert that both are stored
Send the same `PUT` twice and assert that the state equals the state after one
Send one `PUT`, then a `GET`, and compare the body returned with what was sent

questions.prompt: A shop's data and services can fail in ways that no unit test of one function shows. Which kind of check catches each of these first?
hints: Ask whether the fault sits in stored rows, in one service's replies, or between two services.
A fault that only appears when two teams' code meets needs a check that both sides share.

items.label: An order row has a `customer_id` that no customer has
items.explanation: A query can return the orders that point at no customer.

items.label: Two customer rows share an email that the rule says is unique
items.explanation: A grouping query returns the repeated email.

items.label: `GET /orders/999` for a missing order returns `200` with an empty body
items.explanation: The status code is one of the things an API test asserts.

items.label: `POST /orders` with a negative quantity is accepted
items.explanation: An API test sends the bad request and asserts the error status.

items.label: The provider renames `total` to `amount`, and the consumer still reads `total`
items.explanation: Only a check of the real responses against the consumer's expectations sees a rename.

items.label: The provider leaves out `status` for cancelled orders, and the consumer reads it from every reply
items.explanation: Each team's own tests pass, and the contract fails in the provider's build.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The orphan order and the repeated email are data quality checks, the missing order and the negative quantity are API tests, and the renamed field and the missing `status` are contract tests.

questions.onCorrect: Faults in stored rows call for a query, faults in one service's replies call for an API test, and a break between provider and consumer calls for a contract test.

questions.prompt: A not-null check for the `email` column of a `customers` table is written as `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL;` and it returns no rows. What does that mean?
hints: Which rows does the query select?
A check returns the rows that break the rule.

acceptedIdeas: Every row has an email, so the data passes the check
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every row has an email, so the data passes the check

questions.onCorrect: An empty result is a pass, because the check returns only the violations, and a not-null rule is broken only by a row whose `email IS NULL`.

misconceptions.feedback: A check returns the rows that break the rule, so an empty result is the pass; the check would return rows only if some email were missing.
A table with rows in it can pass the check; the result is empty because no row has a `NULL` email, whatever the number of rows.
The check selects exactly the rows whose `email IS NULL`, so any such row would appear in the result.

choices.label: Some rows have no email, but the check hides them
The table is empty
The check is broken, because a working check always returns some rows
Every row has an email, so the data passes the check

questions.prompt: Test A inserts the customer `ada@x` into a shared test database and leaves it there. Test B inserts the same email and expects success. B passes when it runs first and fails with a duplicate error once A has run. What is the best repair?
hints: B's result depends on something A did. Which repair removes that link?
A test is reliable when it creates the data it needs and does not rely on what others left.

acceptedIdeas: Let each test create its own customer with an email unique to that test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Let each test create its own customer with an email unique to that test

questions.onCorrect: When each test makes its own data, no test depends on another, so the order of the run cannot change a result.

misconceptions.feedback: That hides the dependence on order, and it breaks again when someone adds a test or runs one on its own.
A production copy may hold personal information and hides the case under test among millions of rows. It leaves the shared state in place.
That loses a check. The fault is the shared data, and the purpose of the test is sound.

choices.label: Let each test create its own customer with an email unique to that test
Run the tests in a fixed order so that B always goes first
Copy production data into the test database so that the emails look realistic
Delete test B, since it fails

questions.prompt: The twenty response times in ms, sorted, are 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 26, 29, 33, 41, 58, 120 and 450. Suppose the slowest request had taken 4,450 ms instead of 450, and the other nineteen were unchanged. What happens to the mean and the median?
hints: The mean divides the sum of all the times by 20. How much does the sum change?
The median depends on the middle of the sorted list. Does the slowest value move it?

acceptedIdeas: The mean rises by 200 ms and the median stays at 20 ms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mean rises by 200 ms and the median stays at 20 ms

questions.onCorrect: The sum rises by 4,000 ms, so the mean rises by 200 ms, from 48.8 to 248.8 ms. The median, 20 ms, sits between the 10th and 11th values and ignores how slow the slowest request was.

misconceptions.feedback: The median is the middle of the sorted list, here the average of the 10th and 11th values, 19 and 21. The size of the slowest value does not move it.
The extra 4,000 ms is shared among 20 requests, so the mean rises by 4,000 ÷ 20, which is 200 ms.
The mean uses every value, so it rises by 200 ms, from 48.8 to 248.8. Only the median ignores how slow the slowest request was.

choices.label: The mean rises by 200 ms and the median stays at 20 ms
Both rise by 200 ms
The mean rises by 4,000 ms and the median is unchanged
Neither changes, because nineteen of the twenty requests are unchanged

questions.prompt: By nearest rank, what is the 80th percentile of the same twenty times, in ms? Use the sorted list above.
hints: Rank = the percentile as a fraction, times the number of values, rounded up.
Count along the sorted list to that rank.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Four in five of the requests took 33 ms or less, while the slowest fifth stretches all the way to 450 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rank is ceil(0.80 × 20) = 16, and the 16th value of the sorted list is 33 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. A percentile is a value from the list at a given rank.
That is the 15th value. The 80th percentile has rank 16, the next value along.
That is the 18th value, the 90th percentile. The 80th percentile has rank 16.

questions.prompt: A service receives 120 requests per second, and each request spends 0.5 seconds in the system on average. The connection pool holds 40 connections, and each request holds one for its whole time. Is the pool big enough for the average load?
hints: Little's law gives the average number of requests in the system from the arrival rate and the time each spends there.
Compare that average with the 40 connections.

acceptedIdeas: No, because on average 60 requests are in the system at once, more than 40
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because on average 60 requests are in the system at once, more than 40

questions.onCorrect: Little's law gives 120 × 0.5 = 60 requests in the system on average, so with 40 connections about 20 are waiting at any moment. The pool needs 60 or more, and peaks need more again.

misconceptions.feedback: Seconds and connections cannot be compared. Little's law multiplies the rate by the time: 120 × 0.5 gives 60 requests in the system.
The pool has to match the number in the system at once, which is the rate times the time, 120 × 0.5 = 60. The arrival rate alone overstates it.
Quick requests still overlap. With 60 in the system on average, about 20 would be waiting for a connection.

choices.label: No, because on average 60 requests are in the system at once, more than 40
Yes, because 40 connections is more than the 0.5 seconds each request takes
No, because the pool must match the arrival rate of 120 a second
Yes, because requests finish quickly, so 40 connections are always enough

questions.prompt: A load test at the expected demand shows a mean response time of 120 ms, a median of 90 ms and a 95th percentile of 340 ms. The team's target is a 95th percentile under 300 ms. Is the target met?
hints: Which number does the target name?
Compare that number, and no other, with the limit.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the 95th percentile is 340 ms, above the 300 ms limit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the 95th percentile is 340 ms, above the 300 ms limit

questions.onCorrect: The target names the 95th percentile, and 340 ms is above 300 ms, so the system misses it even though its mean and median look fine. A non-functional test is judged against a threshold set beforehand.

misconceptions.feedback: The target names the 95th percentile, which describes the slow tail. The mean hides the slow requests.
The median says half the requests took 90 ms or less. The target is about the slowest 5%.
A load test applies the expected demand, which is the demand the target is stated for. A stress test goes beyond it, to find where the system breaks.

choices.label: Yes, because the mean of 120 ms is well below the 300 ms limit
Yes, because the median of 90 ms is well below the 300 ms limit
It cannot be judged until a stress test has been run as well
No, because the 95th percentile is 340 ms, above the 300 ms limit

questions.prompt: An automated security scanner reports no vulnerabilities in a web application. What does that show?
hints: Ask what the scanner is able to detect.
A clean report can only describe what the tool looks for.

acceptedIdeas: Only that nothing the scanner can detect was found
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only that nothing the scanner can detect was found

questions.onCorrect: A clean report means the tool found nothing it can detect. The remaining problems need manual testing by people.

choices.label: That the application cannot be abused
That the application has been tested against every kind of attack
Only that nothing the scanner can detect was found
That a manual penetration test is no longer needed

misconceptions.feedback: A scanner looks for the kinds of weakness it was built to detect, so the application could still be abused in a way that it does not check.
A scanner covers a part of all the possible attacks, and the rest are outside what it tests.
People find problems that a tool cannot, such as flaws in how the application's rules are designed, so the manual work remains.

questions.prompt: Ten response times in ms, sorted, are 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180 and 900. By nearest rank, what is the 90th percentile?
hints: Rank = the fraction times the number of values, rounded up.
Count to that rank in the sorted list.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The slow request of 900 ms sits at rank 10, so it is left out of the 90th percentile, although it would pull the mean upwards.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rank is ceil(0.90 × 10) = 9, and the 9th value is 180 ms. The 900 sits at rank 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 10th value, which would be the 100th percentile.
That is the mean. A percentile is a value in the list at a given rank.

questions.prompt: Two services are each measured with twenty requests. Service A answers every request in 100 ms. In service B, eighteen requests take 20 ms and two take 820 ms. Both have a mean of 100 ms. Which statement is true?
hints: By nearest rank, the 95th percentile of twenty values is the value at rank 19 of the sorted list.
Compare the mean with the 50th and 95th percentiles of each service.

acceptedIdeas: Service B's 95th percentile is 820 ms, so one request in ten waits far longer than in A
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Service B's 95th percentile is 820 ms, so one request in ten waits far longer than in A

questions.onCorrect: A has every percentile at 100 ms. B has a median of 20 ms and a 95th percentile of 820 ms with the same mean, which is why a team that reports only the mean cannot see B's slow tail.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal means can hide very different tails. B's 95th percentile is 820 ms and A's is 100 ms.
By nearest rank, the 95th percentile of twenty values is the 19th value of the sorted list, which is 820 ms for B and 100 ms for A.
B's median is 20 ms. The mean is pulled up by the two slow requests.

choices.label: The two services perform the same, because their means are both exactly 100 ms
Service B's 95th percentile is 820 ms, so one request in ten waits far longer than in A
Service B has the lower 95th percentile, because most of its requests take 20 ms
Service B's median is 100 ms, because its mean is 100 ms

questions.prompt: A team plans six performance runs for a booking service. Which kind of test is each one?
hints: Ask whether the demand stays at what is expected, goes beyond it, or stays normal for a very long time.
A soak test looks for faults that grow slowly.

items.label: 200 users, the expected demand, for 30 minutes, checking that the 95th percentile stays under 300 ms
items.explanation: It applies the expected demand and checks a target.

items.label: The expected demand for one hour, checking that the error rate stays under 1%
items.explanation: It stays at the expected demand and checks a target.

items.label: Demand raised every minute from 200 users to 2,000, until errors begin
items.explanation: It goes beyond the expected demand to find the breaking point.

items.label: Demand doubled for ten minutes, to see how the service fails and whether it recovers
items.explanation: It pushes past the expected demand and watches how the system fails.

items.label: 200 users for 24 hours, to see whether memory use keeps climbing
items.explanation: It holds a normal load for hours to find a slow leak.

items.label: A steady normal load for three days, watching for connections that are never released
items.explanation: It runs for a long time at normal load, so slow faults can show.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two runs at the expected demand are load tests, the two that push demand beyond it are stress tests, and the two long runs at normal load are soak tests.

questions.onCorrect: Load tests check targets at the expected demand, stress tests look for the breaking point, and soak tests hold a normal load for hours or days to catch slow faults such as leaks.

questions.prompt: A product owner wants a requirement for how fast checkout should be. Which version can a performance test pass or fail?
hints: A test needs a number to compare a result with.
A requirement for speed also has to say under which demand it applies.

acceptedIdeas: The 95th percentile of checkout time stays under 300 ms at 200 orders a minute
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 95th percentile of checkout time stays under 300 ms at 200 orders a minute

questions.onCorrect: A testable requirement names a measure, a threshold and the conditions, so that a run can pass or fail it.

misconceptions.feedback: It names no measure and no threshold, so no run could fail it.
Feeling quick is a judgement, and it names no number to compare a result with.
It names no threshold and no demand, so a small gain would satisfy it.

choices.label: The 95th percentile of checkout time stays under 300 ms at 200 orders a minute
Checkout should be fast enough that customers do not complain about it
Checkout should feel quick to customers on every device they use
Checkout should be noticeably faster than it was in the previous release

questions.prompt: A developer cannot make a crash happen from the report 'Export crashes, see screenshot.' Which addition would help the developer most?
hints: Ask what the developer needs in order to see the crash for themselves.
A screenshot shows the result, and the developer still has to make it happen.

acceptedIdeas: The numbered steps that lead to the crash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The numbered steps that lead to the crash

questions.onCorrect: A fault that can be reproduced can be investigated, whereas one that cannot is usually closed.

choices.label: A guess at which function causes the crash
A second screenshot of the same error message
The numbered steps that lead to the crash
A sentence about how annoying the crash is

misconceptions.feedback: A guess at the cause belongs in a comment, and a wrong guess can send the investigation the wrong way. It gives no way of making the crash happen.
A screenshot shows what happened, and a second one shows the same thing. Neither tells the developer how to make it happen.
How much the crash matters affects the order of fixing, and it gives the developer no way to make it happen.

questions.prompt: Two defects are waiting to be fixed. One loses a customer's saved order, but only in an export feature that a handful of people use. The other shows the wrong date format on the home page, which every visitor sees. The team fixes the date format first. Which statement describes that decision?
hints: Severity is how much harm a defect does.
Priority is the order of fixing, which also depends on how many people see the defect and what else is waiting.

acceptedIdeas: The date format has the higher priority, though the lost order is the more severe
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The date format has the higher priority, though the lost order is the more severe

questions.onCorrect: Severity measures impact and priority sets the order, and they can point in different directions.

misconceptions.feedback: Severity is the impact of a defect, how much harm it does, and the number of people who see it affects priority and not severity.
Losing a customer's order does more harm than a wrong date format, so the lost order is the more severe defect even though it is fixed second.
Priority depends on impact together with other things, such as how many people see a defect and what else is waiting, so it can be higher for the less severe defect.

choices.label: The date format has the higher severity, because more people see it
The date format has the higher priority, though the lost order is the more severe
The two defects have the same severity, and priority only decides the order of work
The date format has the higher priority because it has the higher severity of the two

questions.prompt: Team A found 45 defects before release, and users reported 5 more afterwards. Team B found 30 before release, and users reported 20 more. Which statement is true by defect detection percentage?
hints: The defect detection percentage is the defects found before release divided by the defects found before and after release together.
Work it out for each team and compare.

acceptedIdeas: Team A's is 90% and Team B's is 60%, so A found the larger share before release
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Team A's is 90% and Team B's is 60%, so A found the larger share before release

questions.onCorrect: 45 ÷ 50 is 90% and 30 ÷ 50 is 60%. Each late defect is one that testing missed, so the share found early shows how well testing did.

misconceptions.feedback: Defects reported after release are the ones testing missed, so more of them lowers the percentage.
Both have 50 in all, and A found 45 of them before release where B found only 30.
The percentage is a share of each team's own total, so it compares teams that found different numbers.

choices.label: Team A's is 90% and Team B's is 60%, so A found the larger share before release
Team B did better, because users reported more of its defects
The teams are equal, because each had 50 defects in all
The two cannot be compared, because the teams found different numbers of defects overall

questions.prompt: Team C found 63 defects before release, and users reported 27 more afterwards, so its defect detection percentage is 70%. What is the most useful next step?
hints: Which defects show where testing was weak?
Each late defect was missed by every test that ran.

acceptedIdeas: Study the 27 late defects to see which kind of test was missing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Study the 27 late defects to see which kind of test was missing

questions.onCorrect: The 27 late defects each show a test that was missing, so studying them tells the team where to add checks. 63 ÷ 90 is 70%.

misconceptions.feedback: The percentage compares what testing found with what users found. It says nothing about defects nobody has found yet.
The 30% found late are the evidence that testing missed things. Stopping would let more of them through.
Dropping the late reports would raise the figure to 100% and hide the defects that matter most.

choices.label: Study the 27 late defects to see which kind of test was missing
Report 70% as proof that the product is 70% correct
Stop testing, because 70% of the defects were found
Ignore the later reports and count only the 63 defects found early

questions.prompt: A team releases version 2.4 to 5% of users first, watches the error rate and response times for a day, and then releases it to everyone. What is this practice, and what makes it work?
hints: Who uses the release during the first day, and how does the team learn what happened?
Look for the practice that needs monitoring to be useful.

acceptedIdeas: A canary release, which works because monitoring shows how the 5% fare
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A canary release, which works because monitoring shows how the 5% fare

questions.onCorrect: A canary release shows a new version to a small share of real users, and the monitoring of that group is the evidence for releasing it to everyone.

misconceptions.feedback: A load test applies demand to a test system. A canary uses real users on the live system.
A regression test is an automated check of behaviour that used to work. A canary relies on what real users and monitoring show.
A review reads code before it runs. A canary exposes the running release to a small share of users.

choices.label: A load test, which works because 5% of the demand shows where the limits are
A regression test, which works because the 5% of users repeat earlier bugs
A code review, which works because the 5% of users read the code first
A canary release, which works because monitoring shows how the 5% fare

questions.prompt: Each area gets a risk score, which is likelihood multiplied by impact, each from 1 to 5. Payments have likelihood 2 and impact 5, login has 3 and 4, search has 4 and 2, and the colour theme has 4 and 1. What is the highest score?
hints: Multiply the two numbers for each area.
Compare the four scores.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Login ranks above payments here because its failure is more likely, so it gets testing effort first under these scores.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scores are payments 10, login 12, search 8 and theme 4, so the highest is 12, for login.

misconceptions.feedback: That is payments, whose likelihood is lower than login's.
That adds the two numbers for login. The score is their product.

questions.prompt: Team X made 80 deployments in a month, and 6 needed a fix or a rollback. Team Y made 300 deployments, and 15 needed one. Which team has the lower change failure rate?
hints: A change failure rate divides the failed deployments by all deployments.
Work out each team's rate and compare the two.

acceptedIdeas: Team Y, with 5% against Team X's 7.5%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Team Y, with 5% against Team X's 7.5%

questions.onCorrect: Team Y has 15 ÷ 300, which is 5%, and Team X has 6 ÷ 80, which is 7.5%, so Y's rate is lower even though it had more failed deployments.

misconceptions.feedback: A rate divides the failures by all deployments. Y has 15 ÷ 300, which is 5%, and X has 6 ÷ 80, which is 7.5%.
Both are under 10%, and the rates still differ: Y has 5% and X has 7.5%.
The rate already accounts for how often a team deploys. By it, Y's 5% is lower than X's 7.5%.

choices.label: Team X, because it had fewer failed deployments
Team Y, with 5% against Team X's 7.5%
The two are equal, because both are under 10%
Team X, because it deployed less often and so took fewer risks

questions.prompt: A tester finds that exporting a report crashes. In what order does the crash become a fix with a test that guards it?
hints: Nobody can fix what they cannot reproduce.
The failing test comes before the change that makes it pass.

items: The tester writes numbered steps that reproduce the crash
A developer follows the steps and sees the crash
The developer writes a test that fails for the same reason
The developer changes the code until the test passes
The test stays in the suite to catch the crash if it returns

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tester writes steps to reproduce the crash, the developer sees it, writes a failing test, changes the code until the test passes, and the test stays in the suite.

questions.onCorrect: The report with steps makes the crash reproducible, the failing test captures it, and the passing test then guards the fix for good.

questions.prompt: The app crashes at startup, but only on one phone model that almost none of the customers use. This defect is best described as:
hints: Is the harm large when it happens, and how many people meet it?
Severity is about harm, and priority is about order.

acceptedIdeas: High severity, low priority
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: High severity, low priority

questions.onCorrect: Severity measures the harm when the crash happens, and priority also weighs how many people meet it, so the two can differ.

choices.label: High severity, high priority
Low severity, low priority
High severity, low priority
Low severity, high priority

misconceptions.feedback: Priority also depends on how many people see the defect, and here almost nobody does.
A crash at startup does serious harm to anyone who meets it, so the severity is not low.
A crash at startup does serious harm to anyone who meets it, and the number of customers who meet it is what affects the order of fixing.

questions.prompt: A team ships a release on Monday. On Tuesday it reports a defect detection percentage of 100%, because no defect has been reported since release. What is wrong with the figure?
hints: The measure compares what testing found with what users found later.
How many users have had time to find defects after one day?

acceptedIdeas: Few users have used it yet, so most late defects have not been reported
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Few users have used it yet, so most late defects have not been reported

questions.onCorrect: The measure needs time for users to find things. A figure taken a day after release flatters the team, and it falls as later reports arrive.

misconceptions.feedback: 100% only means that no defect has been reported yet. The figure falls as users find more defects.
With nothing found after release, the share found before release is 100%. The problem lies in the timing, and the formula is fine.
The total of defects found before and after release is not zero, so the division works. It is only too early to trust the result.

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because 100% means that testing found every defect
The percentage should be 0%, because nothing was found after the release
Few users have used it yet, so most late defects have not been reported
The percentage cannot be computed, because it would divide by zero here

flashcards.front: What is the source of the expected result in a test called?
flashcards.back: It is the oracle, and it must be independent of the code under test.

acceptedIdeas: oracle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the oracle, and it must be independent of the code under test.

flashcards.front: What can a green run of 300 tests tell you about a function?
flashcards.back: That it gave the expected result for the 300 inputs tried and raised no error on them. It does not show correctness for every input.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between verification and validation?
flashcards.back: Verification checks the product against its specification, and validation checks that the specification meets the need.

flashcards.front: What do the three parts of a unit test stand for, in order?
flashcards.back: Arrange, act, assert: arrange sets up the input, act calls the code once, and assert states the expected result.

acceptedIdeas: arrange, act, assert
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrange sets up the input, act calls the code once, and assert states the expected result.

flashcards.front: What word means that a test always gives the same result for the same code?
flashcards.back: A deterministic test does not depend on time, order or network, so a failure always means the code changed.

acceptedIdeas: deterministic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A deterministic test does not depend on time, order or network, so a failure always means the code changed.

flashcards.front: Why run a new test against broken code at least once?
flashcards.back: Seeing it fail for the right reason shows that the test can tell good code from bad.

flashcards.front: Free delivery applies to orders of 50 or more. Which two totals are the boundary tests?
flashcards.back: 49 and 50, the value just below the edge and the value at it. A fault such as `total > 50` shows only at 50.

flashcards.front: What do we call a group of inputs that the program should treat alike?
flashcards.back: An equivalence class, so one test from it stands for all of its members.

acceptedIdeas: equivalence class
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An equivalence class, so one test from it stands for all of its members.

flashcards.front: Why does a decision table help when several conditions combine?
flashcards.back: It has one column for every combination of the conditions, so a combination nobody thought of shows up as a missing column.

flashcards.front: What do you call a copy of the code with one small deliberate fault planted in it?
flashcards.back: A mutant, which the suite either kills by failing or lets survive.

acceptedIdeas: mutant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutant, which the suite either kills by failing or lets survive.

flashcards.front: What does a mutant that survives the suite tell you?
flashcards.back: No test noticed that small change, so the suite lacks a check where the mutant differs from the original, often at a boundary.

flashcards.front: Why can a suite with 100% line coverage still be poor?
flashcards.back: Coverage records only that code ran, and a test with no assertion checks nothing.

flashcards.front: What is the practice of passing a unit's dependencies in as arguments called?
flashcards.back: It is dependency injection, and it lets a test supply stand-ins for the clock, the network or a database.

acceptedIdeas: dependency injection
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is dependency injection, and it lets a test supply stand-ins for the clock, the network or a database.

flashcards.front: What separates a stub from a mock?
flashcards.back: A stub returns canned answers, whereas a mock also checks which calls were made to it.

flashcards.front: What is a simple working in-memory stand-in for a database called?
flashcards.back: A fake, which behaves like the real store but is faster and private to the test.

acceptedIdeas: fake
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fake, which behaves like the real store but is faster and private to the test.

flashcards.front: What do you call a statement that holds for every valid input?
flashcards.back: A property, so it can be checked on any generated input.

acceptedIdeas: property
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A property, so it can be checked on any generated input.

flashcards.front: What is it called when a tool reduces a failing input to the smallest one that still fails?
flashcards.back: Shrinking, which leaves the developer with a minimal counter-example.

acceptedIdeas: shrinking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shrinking, which leaves the developer with a minimal counter-example.

flashcards.front: What gives an exploratory testing session its structure?
flashcards.back: A charter that says what to explore and a time box that limits it, plus notes.

flashcards.front: What is the name for changing code structure without changing behaviour?
flashcards.back: Refactoring, whose safety depends on the tests staying green.

acceptedIdeas: refactoring
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Refactoring, whose safety depends on the tests staying green.

flashcards.front: Why watch a new test fail before writing the code?
flashcards.back: A test that has never been seen to fail may be unable to fail, so the red step shows that it checks something.

flashcards.front: What do you call a test written from a bug report so that the bug cannot return?
flashcards.back: A regression test, which fails on the buggy code and passes on the fix.

acceptedIdeas: regression test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A regression test, which fails on the buggy code and passes on the fix.

flashcards.front: What do you call a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code?
flashcards.back: A flaky test, which makes failures harder to trust.

acceptedIdeas: flaky
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A flaky test, which makes failures harder to trust.

flashcards.front: A test passes when run alone and fails in the full suite. What is the likely cause?
flashcards.back: State shared between tests, or a dependence on the order they run in. Each test should build its own data.

flashcards.front: Why should a healthy suite have more unit tests than end-to-end tests?
flashcards.back: Unit tests are fast, cheap and point at the failing piece, while end-to-end tests are slow, brittle and unspecific.

flashcards.front: What do we call a request that has the same effect when repeated as when sent once?
flashcards.back: It is idempotent, so a lost reply can safely be retried.

acceptedIdeas: idempotent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is idempotent, so a lost reply can safely be retried.

flashcards.front: What should a data quality check query return?
flashcards.back: The rows that break the rule, so that an empty result means the data passes.

flashcards.front: Why does a contract test catch a renamed field before release?
flashcards.back: The provider runs the consumer's contract against its real responses in its own build, so the mismatch fails there.

flashcards.front: What does Little's law tell you about a service?
flashcards.back: The average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there, which sizes pools and thread counts.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a test that raises load beyond expected demand to find the breaking point?
flashcards.back: A stress test, which shows where and how the system fails.

acceptedIdeas: stress test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A stress test, which shows where and how the system fails.

flashcards.front: Why can the mean response time mislead?
flashcards.back: A few very slow requests pull the mean up past most of the data, and a percentile shows the slow tail directly.

flashcards.front: What is the word for the impact of a defect, as opposed to the order in which it is fixed?
flashcards.back: Severity measures impact, and priority sets the order of fixing.

acceptedIdeas: severity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Severity measures impact, and priority sets the order of fixing.

flashcards.front: Why is a defect detection percentage taken the day after release unreliable?
flashcards.back: Users have had little time to find defects, so few late reports exist and the figure looks better than it is.

flashcards.front: Why does a team test both early in the pipeline and in production?
flashcards.back: Early tests find defects cheaply, but only real use shows what no test set anticipated.
